97580.e: The nacelle holds the technology that turns the rotation into electricity. It can turn to face the wind.
97580.m: The nacelle sits on top of a wind turbine.

97581.q: Roughly how tall is the tower of a large modern wind turbine?
97581.e: The wind blows more strongly high up. That is why the towers of large wind turbines are often about 100 metres tall or more.
97581.m: Large wind turbines are very tall.

97582.q: How does electricity get from the power station to our homes?
97582.e: Electricity flows through metal lines. That is how it gets from the power station to the socket.
97582.m: Electricity flows to us through lines.

97583.q: Which metal are the wires in household cables often made of?
97583.e: Copper conducts electricity very well. That is why the wires in cables are often made of copper.

97584.q: Why does a cable have a plastic covering on the outside?
a: So that you do not get an electric shock
97584.e: Plastic does not conduct electricity. The covering protects us from the electricity in the wire.
97584.m: A cable's covering protects against electric shocks.

97585.q: What do you do if a power line is lying on the ground?
a: Stay well away and fetch an adult
Pick it up and carry it away
97585.e: A fallen power line may still be live. That is extremely dangerous, so keep your distance.
97585.m: Stay well away from fallen power lines.

97586.q: What are the thick lines that carry electricity over long distances called?
97586.e: For long distances, electricity is sent at a very high voltage. That way less is lost on the way.
97586.m: High-voltage lines carry electricity over long distances.

97587.q: Where do many power lines run in towns?
97587.e: In towns, power cables are mostly in the ground. That way they are protected and do not get in the way.
97587.m: In towns many power cables are underground.

97588.q: What can happen if a storm tears down a power line?
97588.e: If the line is broken, no electricity arrives. Then there is a power cut.
97588.m: A broken line can cause a power cut.

97589.q: Where does the power line in a room end so that you can plug in a device?
97589.e: The lines in the wall lead to the socket. That is where you plug in a device.
97589.m: You get electricity for devices from the socket.

97590.q: What do the large pylons carry?
97590.e: Pylons hold the power lines high above the ground. That way electricity can travel over long distances.

97591.q: What material are large pylons usually made of?
97591.e: Large pylons are made of steel. Steel is very strong and carries the heavy lines.
97591.m: Large pylons are made of steel.

97592.q: Why do power lines hang high up on the pylons?
a: So that nobody can touch them
So that birds can sit on them
97592.e: The lines carry dangerous electricity. High up, nobody can touch them by accident.
97592.m: High lines protect people from electricity.

97593.q: What is always the rule with a pylon?
97593.e: On a pylon you are dangerously close to the lines. Even nearby, the electricity can jump across.

97594.q: What are the parts that the wires hang from on a pylon called?
97594.e: Insulators are made of glass or ceramic. They stop the electricity from flowing into the pylon.
97594.m: Insulators keep the electricity away from the pylon.

97595.q: What material are small electricity poles in the countryside often made of?
97595.e: Wooden poles are enough for smaller lines. You often see them in villages and in the countryside.
97595.m: Small electricity poles are often made of wood.

97596.q: Which large bird sometimes builds its nest on an electricity pylon?
97596.e: Storks like to build their large nests in high places. Sometimes they choose a pylon.
97596.m: Storks like to build their nests high up.

97597.q: How are parts for pylons often taken up into the mountains?
97597.e: There are often no roads in the mountains. A helicopter flies the heavy parts up.
97597.m: In the mountains helicopters help to build pylons.

97598.e: A generator turns a spinning movement into electricity. Every power station has a generator.
97598.m: A generator turns movement into electricity.

97599.q: What can a bike with a generator do when you pedal it?
97599.e: Pedalling turns a generator. That way you can make electricity with your muscles, for example for a lamp.
97599.m: With muscle power and a generator you can make electricity.

97600.q: What is inside a generator so that electricity is produced?
97600.e: When a magnet turns inside a coil of wire, electricity is produced. That is the secret of every generator.
97600.m: Magnets and coils of wire produce electricity in a generator.

97601.q: Why does a hospital have an emergency generator?
a: For electricity during a power cut
For music in the waiting room
97601.e: In a hospital, machines must always keep running. If the power fails, the emergency generator starts up.
97601.m: An emergency generator helps during a power cut.

97602.q: What do you have to do to make a wind-up torch light up?
a: Shake it and blow on it
97602.e: Turning the crank spins a small generator. It makes electricity for the lamp.
97602.m: Turning a crank makes a small generator produce electricity.

97603.q: What happens to a bike light powered by a dynamo when you ride faster?
97603.e: If you ride faster, the dynamo turns faster. Then it makes more electricity.
97603.m: The faster a dynamo turns, the more electricity it makes.

97604.q: Which device does the opposite of a generator and turns electricity into movement?
97604.e: An electric motor uses electricity and turns. A generator turns and makes electricity.
97604.m: An electric motor turns electricity into movement.

97605.q: What does an emergency generator on a building site need to run?
97605.e: Many emergency generators have an engine. It burns diesel and turns the generator.
97605.m: An emergency generator often runs on diesel.

a: A wheel with blades that turns
97606.e: A turbine has many curved blades. When water, steam or gas flows through it, it turns.
97606.m: A turbine is a wheel with blades.

97607.q: What flows through the turbine in a nuclear power station?
97607.e: In a nuclear power station, water is heated into steam. The steam turns the turbine.
97607.m: Hot steam turns the turbine in a nuclear power station.

97608.e: Large aeroplanes have engines with turbines. They push the aeroplane forward powerfully.

97609.q: What flows through the turbine in a gas-fired power station and turns it?
97609.e: In a gas-fired power station, natural gas is burned. The hot exhaust gases rush through the turbine with great force and turn it.
97609.m: In a gas-fired power station hot gas turns the turbine.

97610.q: Which old wheel is an ancestor of the water turbine?
97610.e: Long ago, water already turned large water wheels. The turbine is a modern, faster version of it.
97610.m: The water wheel is the ancestor of the turbine.

97611.q: What are the curved parts of a turbine that the water hits called?
97611.e: The water pushes against the blades. This makes the turbine turn.
97611.m: Water pushes against the blades of a turbine.

97612.q: When does a water turbine turn faster?
a: When more water flows through with more force
97612.e: More water, flowing faster, pushes harder against the blades. Then the turbine turns faster.
97612.m: Lots of water turns a turbine fast.

97613.q: Which machine is the turbine in a power station connected to?
97613.e: The turbine turns the generator. The generator then makes the electricity.

97614.q: At how many places in Switzerland are there nuclear power stations still in operation (as of 2026)?
97614.e: There are nuclear power stations in operation at Beznau, Gösgen and Leibstadt. Beznau has two reactors. Mühleberg was shut down in 2019.
97614.m: In Switzerland nuclear power stations are in operation at three places.

97615.q: What does a nuclear power station need in large amounts for cooling?
97615.e: A nuclear power station has to get rid of a lot of heat. That is why it stands on a river and uses its water for cooling.
97615.m: Nuclear power stations need a lot of cooling water.

97616.q: What rises from the cooling tower as a white cloud?
97616.e: Water vapour rises from the cooling tower. It is a cloud of tiny water droplets, not smoke.
97616.m: Water vapour rises from the cooling tower.

97617.q: Which substance provides the energy in a nuclear power station?
97617.e: In a nuclear power station, uranium atoms are split. This produces a great deal of heat.

97618.q: What is another name for a nuclear power station?
97618.e: In a nuclear power station, atomic nuclei are split. That is why it is also called an atomic power station.
97618.m: A nuclear power station is also called an atomic power station.

97619.q: Which waste from a nuclear power station has to be stored safely for a very long time?
a: Old cooling water from the river
97619.e: Used fuel rods are highly radioactive and give off radiation for a very long time. This radioactive waste must be stored safely.
97619.m: Radioactive waste must be stored safely for a very long time.

97620.q: What is the large round tower at some nuclear power stations called?
97620.e: Water is cooled down in the cooling tower. Gösgen and Leibstadt have cooling towers like this.
97620.m: The cooling tower cools the water down.

97621.q: In which canton is the Gösgen nuclear power station?
97621.e: The Gösgen nuclear power station is in Däniken in the canton of Solothurn. It lies on the Aare.
97621.m: The Gösgen nuclear power station is in the canton of Solothurn.

97622.q: Which Swiss nuclear power station is one of the oldest still running in the world?
97622.e: The first reactor at Beznau has been running since 1969. That makes it one of the oldest in the world still producing electricity.
97622.m: The Beznau nuclear power station is very old.

97623.q: What does an electricity meter measure?
a: How warm it is in the house
97623.e: The electricity meter counts all the electricity used in the house.
97623.m: The electricity meter measures electricity use.

97624.q: In which unit does the electricity meter show how much has been used?
97624.e: Electricity is counted in kilowatt hours. The short form is kWh.
97624.m: Electricity is counted in kilowatt hours.

97625.q: Where is the electricity meter usually found in a house?
a: In the cellar or the stairwell
97625.e: The electricity meter is usually in the cellar or the stairwell. It is often next to the fuses.
97625.m: The electricity meter is usually in the cellar or stairwell.

97626.q: Why do people read the electricity meter?
a: To know how much they have to pay
97626.e: The meter shows how much electricity has been used. The electricity bill is based on that.
97626.m: The electricity meter shows how much electricity you have to pay for.

97627.q: What is a modern electricity meter that sends the readings by itself called?
97627.e: A smart meter is an intelligent electricity meter. It sends the figures to the electricity company by itself.
97627.m: A smart meter sends electricity readings by itself.

97628.q: What turned on old electricity meters when electricity was flowing?
97628.e: Old electricity meters had a flat metal disc. The more electricity flowed, the faster it turned.
97628.m: On old electricity meters a disc turned.

97629.q: When does the electricity meter count especially fast?
a: When many devices are running at the same time
When all devices are switched off
97629.e: Many devices together use a lot of electricity. That is why the meter counts faster then.
97629.m: Many devices make the electricity meter count fast.

97630.q: How can you help the electricity meter count more slowly?
a: Switch off the light when nobody is in the room
Keep the TV on all the time
Turn on all the lamps at once
97630.e: A light that is switched off uses no electricity. So the meter counts less and you save money.
97630.m: Switching off the light saves electricity.

97731.q: How large is the horizontal Coriolis force on a horizontal movement of air directly at the equator?
a: It is half as large as at the pole
97731.e: The Coriolis parameter f is proportional to the sine of the latitude. At the equator sin(0°) equals 0, so there is no horizontal deflection there.
97731.m: At the equator the horizontal Coriolis force disappears.

97732.q: Where on Earth is the horizontal deflection by the Coriolis force greatest?
97732.e: The Coriolis parameter f = 2Ω·sin φ depends on the sine of the latitude. It is greatest at the poles and zero at the equator.
97732.m: Coriolis deflection is strongest at the poles.

97733.q: Why do tropical cyclones not form directly at the equator, but only from about 5° latitude?
a: At the equator there is no Coriolis deflection to make them spin
At the equator the sea is too cold
At the equator there are no thunderstorms
At the equator the air pressure is too high
97733.e: A cyclone needs a deflection so that the inflowing air starts to circle. The horizontal Coriolis force is zero at the equator and only becomes large enough from about 5° latitude.
97733.m: No Coriolis force, no cyclone, which is why there are no hurricanes at the equator.

97734.q: In the Southern Hemisphere, in which direction does the Coriolis force deflect a moving air mass?
97734.e: In the Southern Hemisphere the Coriolis parameter is negative. Moving air is therefore deflected to the left of its direction of motion.
97734.m: In the Southern Hemisphere the Coriolis force deflects to the left.

97735.q: Physically, what kind of force is the Coriolis force?
97735.e: The Coriolis force only appears in a rotating frame of reference such as the Earth. It is therefore a fictitious force and not a real interaction.
97735.m: The Coriolis force is a fictitious force of the rotating frame of reference.

97736.q: Which two forces are in balance in the geostrophic wind?
a: Pressure gradient force and Coriolis force
97736.e: In the free atmosphere without friction from the ground, the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force balance each other. The wind then blows parallel to the isobars.
97736.m: The geostrophic wind blows parallel to the isobars.

97737.q: Why does the Coriolis force have practically no effect on which way water swirls in a washbasin?
a: It is far too weak over short distances and short times
It only acts in the Southern Hemisphere
It only acts on air, not on water
97737.e: The Coriolis force, which Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis described in 1835, only becomes important over large distances and long times, for example in low-pressure systems or ocean currents. In a washbasin, the shape of the basin and small leftover currents decide the direction.
97737.m: In a washbasin, it is not the Coriolis force that decides which way the water swirls.

97738.q: At the North Pole, how long does the plane of swing of a Foucault pendulum take to make one full turn?
97738.e: At the pole the Earth turns once beneath the pendulum in a sidereal day of about 23 hours 56 minutes. At middle latitudes it takes longer because the effect decreases with the sine of the latitude.
97738.m: The Foucault pendulum makes the effect of the Earth's rotation visible.

97739.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, according to Buys Ballot's law, where is the low when you stand with your back to the wind?
a: To the left and slightly ahead
To the right and slightly ahead
97739.e: Because of the deflection to the right, the wind in the Northern Hemisphere flows around a low in such a way that it lies on the left. Because of friction with the ground, it is shifted slightly forwards.
97739.m: In the Northern Hemisphere the low is on your left when the wind is at your back.

97740.q: Which meteorologist are the planetary waves of the westerly wind belt named after?
97740.e: The Swedish-American meteorologist Carl-Gustaf Rossby explained these waves in 1939. They shape the weather of the middle latitudes.
97740.m: Rossby waves bear the name of Carl-Gustaf Rossby.

97741.q: Which effect is the physical basis of Rossby waves?
a: The increase of the Coriolis force with latitude
The decrease of gravity with height
97741.e: Because the Coriolis parameter changes with latitude (the beta effect), air that is shifted north or south experiences a restoring force. This creates waves.
97741.m: The beta effect drives Rossby waves.

97742.q: In which direction do Rossby waves move relative to the basic flow?
97742.e: The phase of Rossby waves moves westwards relative to the average flow. Because the westerly wind is stronger, they often still move slowly eastwards over the ground.
97742.m: Rossby waves move west against the westerly flow.

97743.q: In a Rossby wave, what is the area extending southwards with low pressure at altitude called?
97743.e: The trough is the bulge of cold air to the south with low pressure at altitude. The ridge is the warm bulge to the north.
97743.m: An upper-level trough brings cold air south.

97744.q: What happens to the weather when Rossby waves get a very large amplitude?
a: The flow becomes meridional and weather patterns last longer
The westerlies become stronger and more even
97744.e: With a large amplitude, the air flows strongly north and south. The waves hardly move from the spot, so heat, cold or rain stay in the same place for a long time.
97744.m: Strongly meandering Rossby waves make weather patterns stubborn.

97745.q: Which high-altitude wind follows the Rossby waves at a height of about ten kilometres?
97745.e: The jet stream is a strong band of westerly wind high up. It winds its way around the Earth in troughs and ridges and steers the lows of the middle latitudes.
97745.m: The jet stream winds its way around the Earth with the Rossby waves.

97746.q: How many large Rossby waves typically span the Northern Hemisphere at the same time?
97746.e: The long planetary waves have wavelengths of several thousand kilometres. That is why only a few, typically about three to seven, fit around the hemisphere.
97746.m: Only a few Rossby waves fit around the Earth.

97747.q: Do Rossby waves only occur in the atmosphere?
97747.e: Rossby waves form in every rotating layer of fluid on a sphere. In the oceans they are very slow and take months to years to cross an ocean.
97747.m: The oceans have Rossby waves too.

97748.q: In Ticino, air rises from 400 m at 15 °C, condenses from 1400 m and rises saturated (0.5 °C per 100 m) up to 2400 m. How warm is it when it sinks dry adiabatically to 400 m in the north?
97748.e: Up to 1400 m it cools by 10 °C to 5 °C, and up to 2400 m by another 5 °C to 0 °C. As it descends 2000 m, it warms by 20 °C to 20 °C.
97748.m: With foehn, the air arrives on the lee side warmer than it started on the windward side.

97749.q: During a south foehn, where in Switzerland does the warm, dry downslope wind blow?
a: In the northern Alpine valleys such as the Reuss Valley
97749.e: During a south foehn, Ticino is on the windward side and gets rain. The air descends on the northern side of the Alps into valleys such as the Reuss Valley, the Hasli Valley or the Rhine Valley.
97749.m: During a south foehn it is warm and dry north of the Alps.

97750.q: What is the wall of cloud that stands over the main ridge of the Alps during foehn called?
97750.e: Clouds piled up on the windward side spill over the ridge and dissolve on the lee side. Seen from the north, this looks like a wall.
97750.m: The foehn wall is the wall of cloud over the Alpine ridge.

97751.q: Which lens-shaped clouds often form in the lee of the Alps during foehn?
97751.e: Foehn creates standing lee waves. At the crests of these waves, air condenses into smooth, lens-shaped clouds known as foehn fish.
97751.m: Foehn fish are lens-shaped clouds in lee waves.

97752.q: What is the foehn-like downslope wind on the eastern side of the Rocky Mountains called?
97752.e: The chinook is a warm, dry downslope wind in North America. It can make the temperature rise by more than 20 °C within hours.
97752.m: The chinook is the foehn of the Rocky Mountains.

97753.q: Why can foehn air on the lee side be warm even when it hardly rains on the windward side?
a: It comes from higher air layers that are potentially warmer
It is heated by the rock of the Alps
It is warmed by sunshine in the valley
97753.e: The Alps often block the air near the ground on the windward side. Air from higher up can then descend, and it becomes especially warm as it sinks dry adiabatically.
97753.m: Foehn warmth often comes from sinking air from higher up.

97754.q: During a north foehn, where in Switzerland is the weather warm and dry?
a: On the southern side of the Alps
97754.e: During a north foehn, the air piles up on the northern side of the Alps. In Ticino it descends and brings clear, dry weather.
97754.m: A north foehn brings dry weather to Ticino.

97755.q: What is the cloud-free gap that forms over the Alps on the lee side during foehn called?
97755.e: On the lee side the air sinks and warms up, so clouds dissolve. A bright strip of blue sky appears, the foehn window.
97755.m: In the foehn window the clouds dissolve.

97756.q: What characterises an adiabatic change of state?
a: No heat is exchanged with the surroundings
97756.e: Adiabatic means without heat exchange. Changes in temperature are caused only by compression or expansion.
97756.m: In adiabatic processes, no heat flows across the boundary.

97757.q: By roughly how much does unsaturated air cool as it rises?
97757.e: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is about 9.8 K per kilometre. Rounded, that is 1 °C per 100 m.
97757.m: Dry air cools by about one degree per hundred metres as it rises.

97758.q: Why does saturated air cool more slowly than unsaturated air as it rises?
a: Latent heat is released during condensation
97758.e: When water vapour condenses, heat of vaporisation is released. It slows the cooling to about 0.4 to 0.7 °C per 100 m.
97758.m: The heat of condensation slows the cooling of moist air.

97759.q: Why does a rising parcel of air cool even though no heat is taken away from it?
a: It expands and does work against its surroundings
97759.e: As air pressure decreases, the parcel expands. The work needed for this comes from its internal energy, so its temperature falls.
97759.m: Expansion costs internal energy and cools the air.

97760.q: Why does sinking air warm up, for example during foehn?
a: It is compressed by the rising air pressure
It takes up heat from the ground
The Sun heats it more strongly
It rubs against the mountain slopes
97760.e: As the air sinks, the air pressure rises and the air is compressed. The work of compression increases its internal energy without any heat being added from outside.
97760.m: Sinking air warms up through compression.

97761.q: An unsaturated parcel of air is at 25 °C at the ground and rises 1500 m dry adiabatically. Roughly what temperature does it have?
97761.e: At about 1 °C per 100 m it cools by 15 °C. 25 °C minus 15 °C gives 10 °C.
97761.m: Rising fifteen hundred metres cools dry air by about fifteen degrees.

97762.q: What happens to the air in a bicycle pump when you compress it quickly?
a: It gets warmer because it is compressed
It gets colder because the pressure rises
It gets colder because air escapes
97762.e: When it is compressed quickly there is no time for heat exchange, so the compression is almost adiabatic. The work done raises the temperature, which is why the pump gets warm.
97762.m: Air that is compressed quickly warms up.

97763.q: Why is the saturated adiabatic lapse rate in very cold air close to the dry adiabatic one?
a: Cold air contains little water vapour that can condense
No work is done in cold air
Ice gives off no latent heat
97763.e: The amount of water vapour air can hold falls sharply as the temperature drops. Hardly any heat of condensation is released, so the lapse rate is almost dry adiabatic.
97763.m: In cold air, saturated parcels cool almost as fast as dry ones.

97764.q: What is the layering called when the environmental lapse rate lies between the saturated and the dry adiabatic lapse rates?
97764.e: In this case unsaturated air is stable, but saturated air is unstable. Whether convection develops therefore depends on humidity.
97764.m: Conditionally unstable air only becomes unstable with condensation.

97765.q: In a layer of air the temperature falls by 1.2 °C per 100 m of height. How should the layering be judged?
97765.e: 1.2 °C per 100 m is more than the dry adiabatic lapse rate of about 1 °C per 100 m. A lifted parcel then always stays warmer than its surroundings and keeps rising, even without condensation.
97765.m: A superadiabatic lapse rate means absolute instability.

97766.q: Which temperature lapse rate does the ICAO standard atmosphere assume in the troposphere?
97766.e: The standard atmosphere assumes cooling of 6.5 K per kilometre up to a height of about 11 km. This is an average of real conditions.
97766.m: The standard atmosphere cools by 6.5 kelvin per kilometre.

97767.q: Which type of cloud is typical of unstable layering?
97767.e: With unstable layering, parcels of air keep rising by themselves. This creates tall heaped clouds, up to and including thunderstorms.

97768.q: What does a high CAPE value in a weather forecast indicate?
a: Thick fog in the Swiss Plateau
97768.e: CAPE (Convective Available Potential Energy) measures the energy a rising parcel of air gains through buoyancy. High values indicate the potential for thunderstorms.
97768.m: High CAPE values mean plenty of energy for thunderstorms.

97769.q: Why is the stratosphere very stably layered?
a: The temperature there rises with height
There is no air pressure there
There is no Coriolis force there
97769.e: Ozone absorbs UV radiation and warms the upper layers. Because warm air lies above cold air, vertical mixing is suppressed.
97769.m: Warming by ozone makes the stratosphere stable.

97770.q: Which clouds often form when stable air flows over a mountain and oscillates in waves behind it?
97770.e: In stable air, a displaced parcel oscillates around its resting position; the frequency is called the Brunt-Väisälä frequency. Behind mountains this creates lee waves, and lens-shaped clouds form at their crests, for example during foehn.
97770.m: Lens-shaped clouds show waves in stable air.

97771.q: What happens to a lifted parcel of air in absolutely stable layering?
a: It sinks back to its starting position
It keeps rising faster and faster
It stays put at any height
97771.e: After being lifted, the parcel is colder than its surroundings and therefore heavier. It therefore sinks again.
97771.m: In stable air a lifted parcel returns.

97772.q: How does a subsidence inversion form?
a: Through air sinking and warming in a high
Through the ground radiating heat at night
Through foehn on the windward side
97772.e: In a high-pressure area, air sinks over a large area and warms adiabatically. This creates a warm barrier layer above the cooler air near the ground.
97772.m: Sinking air in a high creates a subsidence inversion.

97773.q: How does a ground inversion form on clear nights?
a: The ground radiates heat and cools the air near the ground
Warm air flows down from above
Clouds keep the heat at the ground
97773.e: Without clouds, the ground gives off a lot of heat as radiation. The lowest layer of air becomes colder than the air above it.
97773.m: Radiation at night creates ground inversions.

97774.q: Why is it often warmer on the Rigi than in Lucerne in winter during an inversion?
a: The Rigi rises above the cold air near the ground
The Rigi is closer to the Sun
There is foehn on the Rigi
The air on mountains is always warmer
97774.e: During an inversion, cold air with high fog collects in the Swiss Plateau. Above it lies warmer, dry air in which mountain tops are sunny.
97774.m: During an inversion the mountains are often warmer than the valley.

97775.q: In which city did an inversion lead to deadly smog in December 1952?
97775.e: In the “Great Smog”, an inversion trapped smoke from coal fires over London for days. Thousands of people died as a result.
97775.m: The “Great Smog” of 1952 showed the danger of inversions.

97776.q: What is a hollow called where cold air collects during an inversion?
97776.e: Cold, heavy air flows into hollows and valleys at night. This creates a cold air pool with a higher risk of frost and fog.
97776.m: Cold air collects in hollows to form a cold air pool.

97777.q: How does an inversion layer affect vertical air movement?
a: Like a lid that stops air from rising
Like a chimney that helps air rise
97777.e: In the inversion the air is warmer at the top than at the bottom and therefore very stable. Rising air is slowed down, and pollutants stay trapped beneath it.
97777.m: An inversion acts as a barrier layer.

97778.q: What often ends a winter inversion in the Swiss Plateau?
a: A passing cold front with wind
97778.e: A cold front brings wind and mixing. As a result, the cold air near the ground is mixed with the air above it and the inversion breaks up.
97778.m: Wind and fronts break up inversions.

97779.q: During an inversion, where is the top of the high fog in the Swiss Plateau usually?
a: At the base of the inversion
97779.e: The moist cold air is capped by the warm layer above it. The blanket of fog therefore ends at the base of the inversion.
97779.m: The high fog ends where the inversion begins.

97780.q: During the First World War, the Briton Lewis Fry Richardson worked out a weather forecast and published it in 1922. What was new about it?
a: He calculated the weather by hand using physical equations
He used the first electronic computer for it
He relied only on old weather lore
He observed the weather with satellites
97780.e: Richardson spent weeks calculating a six-hour forecast by hand. The result was wrong, but the idea of calculating the weather with equations is the basis of today's weather models.
97780.m: In 1922 Richardson was the first to calculate the weather with physical equations.

97781.q: On which computer did the first successful numerical weather forecast run in 1950?
97781.e: Jule Charney, Ragnar Fjørtoft and John von Neumann used ENIAC. It calculated a simplified 24-hour forecast.
97781.m: The first computer weather forecast ran on ENIAC in 1950.

97782.q: What must a computer weather model be fed with before it can calculate a forecast?
a: The current state of the atmosphere from many measurements
The weather data from the same day the previous year
97782.e: Measurements from stations, balloons, aircraft and satellites are combined with a short-range forecast into a starting state. This process is called data assimilation.
97782.m: A weather model starts from the measured state of the atmosphere.

97783.q: Why can a weather model often not calculate individual thunderclouds directly?
a: The clouds are smaller than one grid cell of the model
Clouds cannot be described physically at all
The computers have no memory for clouds
97783.e: A model only calculates average values for each grid cell. Smaller processes such as cloud formation or turbulence are therefore described with simplified approximations.
97783.m: Anything smaller than the model grid has to be described in a simplified way.

97784.q: Why does MeteoSwiss use a particularly fine model grid for Switzerland?
a: So that mountains and narrow Alpine valleys are represented better
Because Switzerland is by the sea
Because coarse grids know nothing about rain
So that the calculation is finished faster
97784.e: In a coarse grid, valleys and peaks disappear. A fine grid of a few kilometres represents the relief of the Alps better, which is important for foehn and thunderstorms, for example.
97784.m: Fine grids represent the Alps better in weather models.

97785.q: Roughly what grid spacing does the finest Swiss weather model, ICON-CH1-EPS, have (as of 2025)?
97785.e: ICON-CH1-EPS calculates with a grid spacing of about 1 km, ICON-CH2-EPS with about 2.1 km. The fine resolution represents the Alpine valleys better.
97785.m: The finest Swiss weather model has a grid of about one kilometre.

97786.q: How does a numerical weather model divide up the atmosphere for its calculations?
a: Into a three-dimensional grid of many small cells
Into a few large climate zones
Only into the layer of air directly above the ground
97786.e: The model calculates temperature, wind, pressure and humidity for each cell in many height layers. The finer the grid, the more accurate it is, but the more computing time it needs.
97786.m: Weather models calculate on a grid of many cells.

97787.q: What does the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), of which Switzerland is a member, provide?
a: Worldwide weather forecasts for several days to weeks
Only avalanche bulletins for the Alps
97787.e: The ECMWF runs one of the best global weather models. National weather services such as MeteoSwiss use its forecasts as a basis.
97787.m: The ECMWF calculates global weather forecasts for the whole of Europe.

97788.q: Which quantities does a radiosonde measure directly as it rises?
97788.e: A radiosonde measures temperature, relative humidity and air pressure, or calculates the pressure. The wind is worked out from its movement.
97788.m: Radiosondes measure temperature, humidity and pressure high up.

97789.q: How is the wind at altitude determined with a modern radiosonde?
a: From GPS tracking of its drift
With a little windmill on the sonde
97789.e: The sonde is carried along by the wind. From its GPS positions, wind direction and wind speed can be calculated at every height.
97789.m: The drift of the radiosonde reveals the wind high up.

97790.q: From which place in Switzerland are MeteoSwiss's radiosondes launched?
97790.e: MeteoSwiss's upper-air station is in Payerne in the canton of Vaud. Radiosondes are launched there regularly.
97790.m: The Swiss radiosondes are launched in Payerne.

97791.q: At which universal times are radiosondes mainly launched simultaneously all over the world?
97791.e: So that measurements can be compared for weather maps and models, the main times are 00 and 12 UTC. They are agreed internationally.
97791.m: Radiosondes are launched worldwide at 00 and 12 UTC.

97792.q: Why does a radiosonde's ascent usually end at a height of about 30 km?
a: The sonde is pulled back from the ground
97792.e: As air pressure falls, the balloon expands more and more. At great height the skin tears, and the sonde falls back on a parachute.
97792.m: The balloon of a radiosonde bursts high up.

97793.q: Which gas are weather balloons for radiosondes filled with?
97793.e: Hydrogen and helium are lighter than air and provide lift. Hydrogen is cheaper, but helium does not burn.
97793.m: Weather balloons rise with hydrogen or helium.

97794.q: What is a diagram called in which a radiosonde ascent is shown as temperature against pressure?
97794.e: An emagram or Skew-T diagram shows temperature and dew point against pressure. Layering and instability can be read from it.
97794.m: Ascents are analysed in thermodynamic diagrams.

97795.q: How does a radiosonde send its measurements?
a: By radio to a ground station
Only after landing, on a memory card
97795.e: The sonde carries a small transmitter and keeps radioing the data to the ground. That is where the name radiosonde comes from.
97795.m: A radiosonde keeps radioing its data to Earth.

97796.q: What distinguishes a supercell from an ordinary thunderstorm cell?
a: It only forms over the sea
97796.e: The updraught of a supercell rotates and is called a mesocyclone. This makes it longer-lasting and more dangerous than a single cell.
97796.m: A supercell has a rotating mesocyclone.

97797.q: Apart from instability, which condition is especially important for supercells?
97797.e: When the wind increases strongly with height and changes direction, horizontal vortices form. The updraught tilts them upright and the cell starts to rotate.

97798.q: What is the typical radar pattern that usually appears on the south-west edge of a supercell called?
97798.e: Rain is carried around the mesocyclone and forms a hook on the radar. It points to strong rotation and possible tornadoes.
97798.m: A hook echo on the radar suggests a supercell.

97799.q: What is the low-hanging, often rotating lowering of cloud beneath a supercell called?
97799.e: The wall cloud forms beneath the updraught, where moist air condenses early. Tornadoes can develop from it.
97799.m: A tornado can develop from a wall cloud.

97800.q: Which dangerous whirl of air can reach down to the ground from the rotating cloud of a supercell?
97800.e: Tornadoes usually form beneath the rotating updraught of a supercell. Typhoons, on the other hand, are huge tropical cyclones over the sea.

97801.q: Why does a thundercloud spread out at the top into a flat anvil?
a: The updraught is stopped at the tropopause
The rain presses the cloud flat
There is no wind at all at the top
The cloud freezes into a sheet of ice at the top
97801.e: At the tropopause the temperature no longer falls with height, so the air hardly rises any further. It therefore flows sideways and forms the typical anvil.
97801.m: The anvil forms where the updraught hits the tropopause.

97802.q: How long can a supercell last?
97802.e: Because the updraught and downdraught are separate, the rain does not choke the updraught. Supercells can therefore stay active for several hours.

97803.q: Why do supercells often bring large hail?
a: The strong updraught keeps hailstones in the cloud for a long time
They contain no liquid water vapour
97803.e: The stronger the updraught, the longer hailstones circle in the supercooled cloud. They grow layer by layer.
97803.m: A strong updraught lets large hailstones grow.

97804.q: In which season is the stratospheric polar vortex at its strongest?
a: In the winter of the respective hemisphere
97804.e: During the polar night, the stratosphere above the pole cools greatly. The temperature contrast drives a powerful vortex of westerly winds.
97804.m: The polar vortex is strongest in winter.

97805.q: What can weaken or split the polar vortex within a few days?
a: A volcanic eruption in the tropics
97805.e: Rising Rossby waves can warm the stratosphere above the pole by several dozen degrees in a few days. The vortex then collapses or splits.
97805.m: A sudden stratospheric warming can destroy the polar vortex.

97806.q: Why is the southern polar vortex usually more stable than the northern one?
a: The Southern Hemisphere has fewer mountains and land-sea contrasts
Antarctica is warmer than the Arctic
There is no Coriolis force in the Southern Hemisphere
97806.e: Mountains and continents stir up planetary waves that disturb the vortex. In the Southern Hemisphere these triggers are weaker.
97806.m: Less wave activity makes the southern polar vortex stable.

97807.q: Which clouds in the Antarctic polar vortex are crucial for the formation of the ozone hole?
97807.e: In the extreme cold, polar stratospheric clouds form. On their surfaces, chlorine is activated, which destroys ozone in spring.
97807.m: Polar stratospheric clouds promote ozone depletion.

97808.q: Seen from above, in which direction does the polar vortex turn in the Northern Hemisphere?
97808.e: The polar vortex is a large low with westerly winds. In the Northern Hemisphere, cyclonic systems turn anticlockwise.
97808.m: The northern polar vortex turns anticlockwise.

97809.q: What effect can a disturbed polar vortex have on Europe a few weeks later?
a: More tropical cyclones in the Atlantic
97809.e: After a collapse, the westerly flow can also weaken in the troposphere. Arctic cold air then pushes south more often.
97809.m: A weakened polar vortex can bring cold to Europe.

97810.q: Why does the ozone hole form mainly over Antarctica and less over the Arctic?
a: The Antarctic polar vortex is more stable and colder
There are more factories over Antarctica
Antarctica is closer to the Sun
There is no ozone over the Arctic
97810.e: Polar stratospheric clouds, on which chlorine is activated, only form in extreme cold of about minus 78 degrees. Such temperatures are reached mainly in the stable Antarctic vortex.
97810.m: The cold, stable polar vortex makes Antarctica prone to the ozone hole.

97811.q: What mainly disturbs the polar vortex?
97811.e: In winter, Rossby waves from the troposphere rise into the stratosphere. They slow the vortex down and push it away from the pole.
97811.m: Planetary waves disturb the polar vortex from below.

97812.q: Where does the omega block get its name from?
a: The upper-level flow looks like the Greek letter Ω
It occurs at the end of the year
It was described by a researcher called Omega
It is the last phase of a low
97812.e: On the upper-air weather map, the flow goes around a strong high in a wide arc to the north. The contour lines therefore resemble the capital letter omega.
97812.m: On the map the omega block looks like an Ω.

97813.q: How is an omega block structured?
a: A high lies between two lows
A low lies between two highs
Two highs lie on top of each other
A low lies directly over the pole
97813.e: In the centre is a strong high, flanked by a low to the west and one to the east. This arrangement is very persistent.
97813.m: In an omega block a high lies between two lows.

97814.q: Which group of weather patterns does the omega block belong to?
97814.e: The omega block blocks the usual westerly flow. Lows from the Atlantic are steered around the high.
97814.m: The omega block is a typical blocking pattern.

97815.q: What weather does an omega block usually bring in the area of the high in summer?
97815.e: In the high, air sinks and clouds dissolve. Because the pattern stays put, heat can build up over many days.
97815.m: In summer an omega block can bring long periods of heat.

97816.q: Which heatwave in Europe was largely caused by a blocking omega pattern?
97816.e: In summer 2003 a stationary high lay over central Europe. It brought weeks of heat and drought, in Switzerland too.
97816.m: The heat of 2003 developed under a blocking high.

97817.q: What weather is often found on the flanks of the high in an omega block?
97817.e: The two lows also stay in the same place for a long time. As a result it rains beneath them for days, which can cause flooding.
97817.m: On the flanks of an omega block it often rains for a long time.

97818.q: Which country experienced record heat and large forest and peat fires in summer 2010 because of a blocking pattern lasting weeks?
97818.e: In summer 2010 a high over western Russia blocked the westerly flow for weeks. This led to record heat and large fires around Moscow.
97818.m: In 2010 a blocking pattern brought record heat to Russia.

97819.q: Why is an omega block difficult for weather services to forecast?
a: It is hard for models to get the start and end of the block right
It is invisible on satellite images
It only lasts a few hours
97819.e: Weather models struggle to time correctly when a block forms and especially when it breaks down. The uncertainty is therefore higher than with westerly patterns.
97819.m: Blocking patterns are hard for weather models to forecast.

a: Many model runs with slightly changed starting conditions
A single run with a very fine grid
A forecast made only from measurements
The average of all climate data
97820.e: Small differences in the starting state grow in the atmosphere. Many slightly disturbed runs show how large the uncertainty is.
97820.m: An ensemble consists of many slightly different model runs.

97821.q: Why do weather services calculate the same forecast dozens of times with slightly changed starting values?
a: To estimate how certain the forecast is
Because the first run is always wrong
97821.e: The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, for example, calculates 51 runs. If the results are close together, the forecast is reliable.
97821.m: Many model runs show how uncertain a forecast is.

97822.q: What does a large spread of the ensemble members tell you?
a: The model has been programmed incorrectly
97822.e: If the members drift far apart, the weather situation reacts sensitively to small errors. The forecast is then uncertain.
97822.m: A large spread means great uncertainty.

97823.q: What is the ensemble run without disturbed starting conditions called?
97823.e: The control run starts with the unchanged analysis. The other members are given small disturbances.
97823.m: The control run is the undisturbed ensemble member.

97824.q: In 15 of 50 ensemble members it rains at a place. What is the probability of rain?
97824.e: 15 divided by 50 gives 0.3. This corresponds to a probability of 30 %.
97824.m: The probability is the share of members that show the event.

97825.q: Which researcher showed in 1963 that tiny differences in starting conditions can make weather forecasts useless?
97825.e: Edward Lorenz discovered the chaotic behaviour of simple weather models. This gave rise to the image of the butterfly effect.
97825.m: Lorenz discovered chaos in weather forecasting.

97826.q: What is the graph called in which one contour line from every ensemble member is drawn on top of the others?
97826.e: Each member provides its own line. If they lie close together, the situation is certain; if they drift apart, the picture looks like spaghetti.
97826.m: A spaghetti plot shows the spread of an ensemble.

97827.q: Why does MeteoSwiss use a particularly fine weather model for Switzerland?
a: Because the Alps change the weather a lot over a small area
Because no weather comes into Switzerland from abroad
Because Switzerland is by the sea
97827.e: Mountains, valleys and lakes affect wind, rain and temperature over just a few kilometres. Models such as ICON-CH1-EPS therefore calculate with a grid of about one kilometre.
97827.m: The Alps call for especially fine weather models.

97828.q: Apart from uncertain starting values, how do ensembles also take errors in the model itself into account?
a: Through random disturbances in the model physics
By using a coarser grid for all runs
By calculating without the Coriolis force
97828.e: Many ensembles use stochastic physics or different parameterisations. This also captures the uncertainty of the model.
97828.m: Ensembles also disturb the model physics to represent model errors.

97829.q: How does the relative humidity typically change when foehn sets in in a valley north of the Alps?
97829.e: The sinking air warms up without taking up moisture. As a result the relative humidity often falls below 30 %, which increases the risk of fire.
97829.m: Foehn air is warm and very dry.

97830.q: At what speed does a radiosonde balloon typically rise?
97830.e: The amount of gas is chosen so that the balloon rises at about 5 m/s. The ascent to about 30 km therefore takes around 1.5 to 2 hours.
97830.m: A weather balloon rises at about five metres per second.

97831.q: Why do the boiling points of the unbranched alkanes rise as the chain gets longer?
a: The van der Waals forces between the molecules increase
97831.e: Longer molecules have a larger surface area and more electrons. As a result, the van der Waals forces become stronger and more energy is needed to evaporate them.
97831.m: The longer the alkane chain, the higher the boiling point.

97832.q: Which unbranched alkane is the first in the series to be liquid at room temperature?
97832.e: Butane boils at about −0.5 °C and is a gas at 20 °C. Pentane boils at about 36 °C and is therefore liquid.
97832.m: From pentane on, the unbranched alkanes are liquid at room temperature.

97833.q: Why does 2,2-dimethylpropane have a lower boiling point than pentane, even though both are C₅H₁₂?
a: The ball-shaped molecule has less contact area
97833.e: Branched molecules are more compact and touch each other less. So the van der Waals forces are weaker and the boiling point falls.
97833.m: Branching lowers the boiling point of alkanes.

97834.q: Which substance, with an octane number of 100, is the reference for petrol?
97834.e: 2,2,4-Trimethylpentane, also called isooctane, resists knocking very well and is given the octane number 100. n-Heptane is given the octane number 0.
97834.m: By definition, isooctane has an octane number of 100.

97835.q: What is the unbranched alkane with the molecular formula C₇H₁₆ called?
97835.e: Seven carbon atoms give the stem “hept”. With the ending “-ane”, the alkane is called heptane.

97836.q: What is the general molecular formula of the ring-shaped cycloalkanes?
97836.e: Closing the ring needs an extra C-C bond, and two hydrogen atoms are lost in return. Cyclohexane, for example, has the formula C₆H₁₂.
97836.m: Cycloalkanes have two hydrogen atoms fewer than open-chain alkanes.

97837.q: How many oxygen molecules are needed to burn one molecule of propane (C₃H₈) completely?
97837.e: C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ gives 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O. On the right there are 6 + 4 equals 10 oxygen atoms, so 5 O₂ are needed.
97837.m: One propane molecule burns with five oxygen molecules.

97838.q: Roughly what is the molar mass of hexane (C₆H₁₄) (C: 12.0 g/mol, H: 1.0 g/mol)?
97838.e: 6 · 12.0 g/mol plus 14 · 1.0 g/mol gives 72 + 14 equals 86 g/mol.
97838.m: Hexane has a molar mass of about 86 grams per mole.

97839.q: Why do alkanes practically not dissolve in water?
97839.e: Alkanes contain only non-polar C-C and C-H bonds. They cannot form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
97839.m: Non-polar alkanes do not mix with water.

97840.q: What is the general molecular formula of alkenes with one double bond?
97840.e: A double bond replaces two hydrogen atoms. So alkenes have two H fewer than the corresponding alkanes.
97840.m: Alkenes have twice as many hydrogen atoms as carbon atoms.

97841.q: According to Markovnikov's rule, which main product forms when HBr adds to propene?
97841.e: The hydrogen atom goes to the double-bond C atom with more hydrogen. This forms the more stable secondary carbocation, and the bromine ends up on the middle C atom.
97841.m: According to Markovnikov, the hydrogen goes where there is already more hydrogen.

97842.q: What is the alkene with the formula CH₂=CH-CH₃ called?
97842.e: Three carbon atoms give “prop”, and the ending “-ene” stands for the double bond. No position number is needed here.
97842.m: Propene is the alkene with three carbon atoms.

97843.q: Which product forms when water is added to ethene?
97843.e: In hydration, an H atom and an OH group add to the double bond. This is how ethanol is made industrially.

97844.q: Which alkene acts as a hormone in plants for ripening fruit?
97844.e: Ripe apples and bananas give off ethene. It speeds up the ripening of nearby fruit.

97845.q: What forms when an alkene reacts with hydrogen and a nickel catalyst?
97845.e: In hydrogenation, hydrogen is added to the double bond. The process is used, for example, to harden fats for margarine.

97846.q: Which test shows double bonds by decolourising purple potassium permanganate?
97846.e: Alkenes are oxidised to diols by potassium permanganate. The purple colour disappears and brown manganese dioxide forms.

97847.q: Which types of bond make up a C=C double bond?
a: One σ bond and one π bond
One ionic bond and one σ bond
97847.e: The σ bond lies on the axis between the atoms, the π bond above and below it. The π bond is weaker and more reactive.
97847.m: A double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond.

97848.q: Which diene is the building block of natural rubber?
97848.e: Natural rubber is a polymer made of isoprene units. Isoprene has two double bonds.
97848.m: Natural rubber is built from isoprene.

97849.q: What is the general molecular formula of alkynes with one triple bond?
97849.e: Compared with the alkane, a triple bond replaces four hydrogen atoms. That leaves 2n − 2 hydrogen atoms.
97849.m: Alkynes have four hydrogen atoms fewer than alkanes.

97850.q: By which common name is ethyne known?
97850.e: In everyday life, ethyne (C₂H₂) is called acetylene. Ethylene, on the other hand, is the common name of ethene.

97851.q: What is ethyne mainly used for together with oxygen?
97851.e: The flame of ethyne with oxygen reaches over 3,000 °C. It can be used to weld and cut steel parts.
97851.m: Ethyne produces a very hot welding flame.

97852.q: From which solid and water is ethyne produced, for example in a carbide lamp?
97852.e: CaC₂ + 2 H₂O gives C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂. The gas produced burns with a bright flame.
97852.m: Calcium carbide gives off ethyne with water.

97853.q: What molecular geometry do the carbon atoms at a C≡C triple bond have?
97853.e: The two σ bonds of each carbon atom point in opposite directions. That is why the atoms H-C≡C-H lie on a straight line.
97853.m: At a triple bond, the molecule is linear.

97854.q: What hybridisation do the carbon atoms in ethyne have?
97854.e: One s orbital and one p orbital each combine to form two sp orbitals. The two remaining p orbitals form the two π bonds.
97854.m: The carbon atoms in ethyne are sp hybridised.

97855.q: Why is ethyne stored dissolved in acetone in gas cylinders?
a: Pure, compressed ethyne can break down explosively
97855.e: Under pressure, ethyne can break down by itself into carbon and hydrogen. Dissolved in acetone in a porous mass, it can be stored safely.
97855.m: Ethyne is stored dissolved in acetone.

97856.q: What is the molecular formula of propyne?
97856.e: Propyne is propane with four hydrogen atoms fewer. It has the structure HC≡C-CH₃.
97856.m: Propyne has the molecular formula C₃H₄.

97857.q: Which group does propan-2-ol belong to?
97857.e: The C atom with the OH group is bonded to two other carbon atoms. So propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol.
97857.m: In secondary alcohols, the OH carbon carries two carbon groups.

97858.q: Why can 2-methylpropan-2-ol hardly be oxidised with mild oxidising agents?
a: There is no hydrogen atom on the C atom with the OH group
It is not soluble in water
97858.e: In tertiary alcohols, the C atom with the OH group carries three carbon groups. Without an H atom there, no C=O group can form.
97858.m: Tertiary alcohols are hard to oxidise.

97859.q: Why is drinking methanol so dangerous?
a: The body turns it into poisonous substances that can cause blindness
97859.e: In the liver, methanol is turned into formaldehyde and formic acid. These damage the optic nerve, among other things.
97859.m: Methanol is dangerously poisonous even in small amounts.

97860.q: How does the solubility of alkanols in water change as the chain gets longer?
a: It first decreases, then increases again
97860.e: The OH group is hydrophilic and the alkyl chain hydrophobic. The longer the chain, the more the non-polar part dominates.

97861.q: Why does ethanol (78 °C) boil at a much higher temperature than propane (−42 °C), which has about the same mass?
97861.e: The OH groups link ethanol molecules through hydrogen bonds. These are much stronger than the van der Waals forces in propane.
97861.m: Hydrogen bonds raise the boiling point of alcohols.

97862.q: Which dihydric alcohol is used as antifreeze in car radiators?
97862.e: Ethane-1,2-diol has two OH groups and mixes well with water. It greatly lowers the freezing point of the cooling water.
97862.m: Ethylene glycol stops cooling water from freezing.

97863.q: What is glycerol called in IUPAC nomenclature?
97863.e: Glycerol has three carbon atoms, each with one OH group. This gives the name propane-1,2,3-triol.

97864.q: Which products form when ethanol reacts with sodium?
97864.e: The sodium replaces the H atom of the OH group. Sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas are formed.
97864.m: Alcohols form alkoxides and hydrogen with sodium.

97865.q: What is the simplest aldehyde called?
97865.e: Methanal has the formula HCHO. Its solution in water is called formalin and is used as a preservative.

97866.q: Which ending do aldehydes have in IUPAC nomenclature?
97866.e: Aldehydes get the ending “-al”, as in ethanal. Alcohols end in “-ol”, ketones in “-one”.

97867.q: Which aldehyde forms when ethanol is mildly oxidised?
97867.e: Ethanol is a primary alcohol. Mild oxidation produces ethanal (acetaldehyde).
97867.m: Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes.

97868.q: What do you observe in a positive Fehling's test with an aldehyde?
97868.e: The aldehyde reduces copper(II) ions to copper(I) oxide. This is precipitated as a brick-red solid.
97868.m: Fehling's test produces red copper(I) oxide.

97869.q: What is the test called in which an aldehyde produces a silver mirror on the glass?
97869.e: The aldehyde reduces silver ions in ammoniacal solution to elemental silver. This is deposited as a mirror.
97869.m: Tollens' test produces a silver mirror.

97870.q: Which class of substances are aldehydes oxidised further to?
97870.e: The aldehyde group -CHO takes up an oxygen atom and becomes the carboxyl group. In this way, ethanal turns into acetic acid.
97870.m: Aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids.

97871.q: Which aromatic aldehyde smells of bitter almonds?
97871.e: Benzaldehyde consists of a benzene ring with a CHO group. It gives the typical smell of bitter almonds and marzipan.

97872.q: Which aldehyde is the main flavour substance of vanilla?
97872.e: Besides the aldehyde group, vanillin has a hydroxyl group and a methoxy group on the benzene ring. Today it is mostly made synthetically.

97873.q: What is the simplest ketone called in IUPAC nomenclature?
97873.e: Propanone (acetone) has three carbon atoms with the carbonyl group in the middle. A ketone needs at least three C atoms.

97874.q: Why does a ketone need at least three carbon atoms?
a: The carbonyl C must be bonded to two other carbon atoms
Ketones always have two C=O groups
97874.e: In ketones, the C=O group is inside the chain. There must be a carbon group on each side.
97874.m: In ketones, the carbonyl group lies between two carbon groups.

97875.q: Which class of substances forms when a secondary alcohol is oxidised?
97875.e: The C atom with the OH group carries two carbon groups. Oxidation creates a C=O group inside the chain, so a ketone.
97875.m: Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones.

97876.q: How do ketones behave in Fehling's test?
a: They turn the solution brick red
97876.e: Ketones have no hydrogen atom on the carbonyl C and are not easily oxidised. The blue Fehling's solution stays unchanged.
97876.m: Fehling's test tells aldehydes and ketones apart.

97877.q: What is acetone often used for in the home?
97877.e: Acetone dissolves many synthetic resins and varnishes. It mixes with water and evaporates quickly.

97878.q: What is the ketone with four carbon atoms called?
97878.e: With four C atoms, the carbonyl group can only be on the second C atom. So no position number is needed.
97878.m: Butanone is the ketone with four carbon atoms.

97879.q: Why does acetone (56 °C) boil at a lower temperature than propan-2-ol (82 °C)?
a: Acetone molecules do not form hydrogen bonds with each other
97879.e: Acetone has no H atom bonded to oxygen. Only dipole-dipole forces act, and these are weaker than hydrogen bonds.
97879.m: Ketones boil at lower temperatures than comparable alcohols.

97880.q: What is the equilibrium between a ketone and its form with a C=C double bond and an OH group called?
97880.e: An H atom moves from the neighbouring C to the oxygen and the double bond shifts. With simple ketones, the equilibrium lies almost entirely on the keto side.
97880.m: Ketones are in equilibrium with their enol form.

97881.q: What is the common name of methanoic acid?
97881.e: Methanoic acid (HCOOH) was first obtained from ants. It is also found in stinging nettles.
97881.m: Methanoic acid is also called formic acid.

97882.q: Which carboxylic acid is responsible for the smell of rancid butter?
97882.e: Butanoic acid is released when butterfat breaks down. It smells unpleasantly rancid, which is why it is also called butyric acid.
97882.m: Butyric acid makes rancid butter smell.

97883.q: Which acid is stronger: methanoic acid (pKa 3.75) or ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76)?
a: Neither of them is an acid
97883.e: A smaller pKa means a stronger acid. The methyl group of ethanoic acid pushes electrons towards the carboxyl group and weakens it.
97883.m: The smaller the pKa, the stronger the acid.

97884.q: Because of its structure, which carboxylic acid also gives a positive Tollens' test?
97884.e: In the HCOOH molecule there is a hydrogen atom on the carboxyl C, as in an aldehyde. So methanoic acid acts as a reducing agent and is oxidised to carbon dioxide.
97884.m: Methanoic acid is reducing because of its H atom on the carboxyl carbon.

97885.q: Why do carboxylic acids have especially high boiling points?
a: Pairs of molecules form dimers through hydrogen bonds
97885.e: Two carboxyl groups join through two hydrogen bonds to form a double molecule. More energy has to be supplied to evaporate them.
97885.m: Carboxylic acids form dimers through hydrogen bonds.

97886.q: Which dicarboxylic acid is found in large amounts in rhubarb leaves?
97886.e: Oxalic acid (ethanedioic acid) consists of two linked carboxyl groups. Rhubarb and wood sorrel contain a lot of it.

97887.q: What are the salts of acetic acid called?
97887.e: When acetic acid gives off its proton, the acetate ion CH₃COO⁻ forms. One example is sodium acetate.
97887.m: Salts of acetic acid are called acetates.

97888.q: Which aromatic carboxylic acid is used as the preservative E 210?
97888.e: Benzoic acid stops yeasts and moulds from growing. It consists of a benzene ring with a carboxyl group.

97889.q: Which structural group is typical of esters?
a: -CHO at the end of the chain
97889.e: In an ester, a carbonyl group is joined through an oxygen atom to a second carbon group. This group is called the ester group.
97889.m: Esters have the group -COO- between two groups.

97890.q: Which fruit does 3-methylbutyl acetate (isoamyl acetate) smell of?
97890.e: Isoamyl acetate is an ester of acetic acid and 3-methylbutan-1-ol. It is used as banana flavouring.

97891.q: Which ester of salicylic acid and methanol smells of wintergreen and is found in sports creams?
97891.e: Methyl salicylate is the methyl ester of salicylic acid. It is found in oil of wintergreen and is used in rubs.

97892.q: Chemically speaking, which substances are esters of glycerol and three fatty acids?
97892.e: Glycerol binds three fatty acids through its three OH groups. Such triglycerides are the main components of fats and oils.

97893.q: Why do esters boil at lower temperatures than carboxylic acids of the same molecular mass?
a: Esters do not form hydrogen bonds with each other
97893.e: The ester group lacks the H atom bonded to oxygen. Only weaker dipole-dipole forces act between the molecules.
97893.m: Esters are more volatile than carboxylic acids.

97894.q: What do natural waxes such as beeswax mainly consist of?
a: Esters of long-chain acids and long-chain alcohols
97894.e: In waxes, a long-chain fatty acid is esterified with a long-chain monohydric alcohol. This makes them solid and water-repellent.
97894.m: Waxes are esters of long acids and long alcohols.

97895.q: Which well-known medicine is an ester of acetic acid with salicylic acid?
97895.e: In acetylsalicylic acid, the OH group of salicylic acid is esterified with acetic acid. It relieves pain and lowers fever.

97896.q: Which ester forms from acetic acid and ethanol?
97896.e: In esterification, the acid group of acetic acid reacts with the OH group of ethanol, and water is split off. Ethyl acetate smells fruity and is used as a solvent, for example in nail polish remover.
97896.m: Acetic acid and ethanol form the ester ethyl acetate.

97897.q: How are primary, secondary and tertiary amines distinguished?
a: By the number of carbon groups on the nitrogen
By the number of double bonds
97897.e: A primary amine has one, a secondary two and a tertiary three carbon groups on the N atom. So triethylamine is tertiary.
97897.m: The number of groups on the nitrogen decides the type of amine.

97898.q: Why do amines react as bases in water?
a: The lone pair on the nitrogen takes up a proton
97898.e: Like ammonia, amines bind an H⁺ to their lone pair. This produces hydroxide ions in the solution.

97899.q: Which amine is responsible for the typical smell of fish?
97899.e: Trimethylamine forms when fish protein breaks down. Lemon juice binds it as a salt and reduces the smell.

97900.q: What is the simplest aromatic amine called?
97900.e: Aniline (phenylamine) consists of a benzene ring with an NH₂ group. It was the starting material for many synthetic dyes.
97900.m: Aniline is the simplest aromatic amine.

97901.q: What forms when methylamine reacts with hydrochloric acid?
97901.e: The amine takes up the proton of the acid and becomes the methylammonium ion. With the chloride ion it forms a salt.
97901.m: Amines form ammonium salts with acids.

97902.q: Why does methylamine (about −6 °C) boil at a lower temperature than methanol (about 65 °C)?
a: The N-H hydrogen bonds are weaker than the O-H bonds
97902.e: Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen. So the hydrogen bonds of amines are weaker.
97902.m: Amines boil at lower temperatures than comparable alcohols.

97903.q: Which functional group does a primary amine have?
97903.e: The amino group consists of a nitrogen atom with two hydrogen atoms. It is bonded to a carbon group.
97903.m: Primary amines have an NH₂ group.

97904.q: Which two amines form when protein rots and have a very unpleasant smell?
97904.e: Bacteria break down the amino acids ornithine and lysine into putrescine and cadaverine. Both are diamines with a strong smell of decay.
97904.m: The smell of decay comes partly from diamines.

97905.q: According to Hückel's rule, how many π electrons must a flat ring contain to be aromatic?
97905.e: A planar, fully conjugated ring is aromatic if it has 4n + 2 π electrons. Benzene meets this with six π electrons.

97906.q: Which aromatic compound made of two joined benzene rings used to be used in mothballs?
97906.e: Naphthalene (C₁₀H₈) consists of two fused benzene rings. It sublimes and has a strong smell.
97906.m: Naphthalene consists of two joined benzene rings.

97907.q: What is the common name of methylbenzene?
97907.e: Toluene is benzene with a methyl group. It is an important solvent and less poisonous than benzene.

97908.q: How many structural isomers of dimethylbenzene (xylene) are there?
97908.e: The two methyl groups can be in the ortho, meta or para position. This gives three isomers.
97908.m: Disubstituted benzenes come in ortho, meta and para forms.

97909.q: Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?
a: The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance in the ring
97909.e: The negative charge of the phenoxide ion spreads over the benzene ring. This makes it easier to release the proton.
97909.m: Phenol is more acidic than ordinary alcohols.

97910.q: Which type of reaction is typical of aromatic compounds?
97910.e: In a substitution, the stable aromatic electron system is kept. An addition would destroy it.
97910.m: Aromatic compounds prefer substitution to addition.

97911.q: Which polycyclic aromatic compound is a highly carcinogenic component of tobacco smoke and charred barbecued food?
97911.e: Benzo[a]pyrene consists of five fused rings. It forms when organic substances burn incompletely.

97912.q: Which aromatic compound with a vinyl group is the building block of polystyrene?
97912.e: Styrene (vinylbenzene) has a C=C double bond next to the ring. It is polymerised through this bond to form polystyrene.

97913.q: Which six-membered ring containing nitrogen is also aromatic?
97913.e: In pyridine, an N atom replaces one CH group of benzene. The ring stays planar with six π electrons.
97913.m: Pyridine is a heterocyclic aromatic compound.

97914.q: Who proposed the ring structure of benzene in 1865?
97914.e: August Kekulé described benzene as a six-membered ring with alternating single and double bonds. He later told of a dream about a snake.
97914.m: Kekulé recognised the benzene ring in 1865.

97915.e: Michael Faraday obtained benzene from the residues of lighting gas. He determined the ratio of carbon to hydrogen.

97916.q: How long are the C-C bonds in benzene compared with single and double bonds?
a: All the same length, in between
All as long as single bonds
All as short as double bonds
97916.e: All six bonds are about 139 pm long. That lies between the C-C single bond (154 pm) and the C=C double bond (134 pm).
97916.m: In benzene, all the ring bonds are the same length.

97917.q: Cyclohexene has an enthalpy of hydrogenation of -120 kJ/mol, benzene one of -208 kJ/mol. Roughly how large is the resonance energy of benzene?
97917.e: For three isolated double bonds you would expect 3 · (-120) = -360 kJ/mol. The difference from -208 kJ/mol is 152 kJ/mol.
97917.m: Benzene is about 150 kJ/mol more stable than expected.

97918.q: Why is benzene hardly used as a solvent any more?
97918.e: Benzene can damage the blood-forming bone marrow and cause leukaemia. It is usually replaced by toluene.

97919.q: Which catalyst is typically used for the bromination of benzene with bromine?
97919.e: Iron(III) bromide is a Lewis acid and polarises the bromine molecule. Only then is it electrophilic enough to react with the benzene ring to form bromobenzene.
97919.m: Benzene only reacts with bromine when a Lewis acid is used as a catalyst.

97920.q: What is the maximum amount of benzene petrol may contain in Switzerland and the EU (as of 2025)?
97920.e: Because of the health risk, the benzene content of petrol is limited to 1 per cent by volume. It used to be much higher.
97920.m: Petrol may contain at most one per cent benzene.

97921.q: At roughly what temperature does benzene boil?
97921.e: Benzene boils at about 80 °C and melts at about 5.5 °C. At room temperature it is a colourless liquid.
97921.m: Benzene boils at about 80 degrees Celsius.

97922.q: What shape is a benzene molecule?
97922.e: All the carbon atoms are sp² hybridised and lie in one plane with the H atoms. The bond angles are 120°.
97922.m: The benzene molecule is a flat hexagon.

97923.q: What is meant by a functional group?
a: A group of atoms that shapes the properties and reactions of a molecule
The longest carbon chain of a molecule
The total number of hydrogen atoms
97923.e: Functional groups such as -OH or -COOH determine chemical behaviour. Organic substances are sorted into classes of compounds according to them.
97923.m: Functional groups determine the class of compound.

97924.q: Which functional group do aldehydes and ketones have in common?
97924.e: Both classes contain a carbon-oxygen double bond. They differ only in its position in the chain.
97924.m: Aldehydes and ketones are carbonyl compounds.

97925.q: Which class of compounds has the general structure R-O-R'?
97925.e: In ethers, an oxygen atom is bonded between two carbon groups. One example is diethyl ether.
97925.m: Ethers have an oxygen atom between two groups.

97926.q: Which class of compounds carries the functional group -CONH₂?
97926.e: In amides, a nitrogen atom is bonded directly to a carbonyl group. Amines lack this C=O group.
97926.m: Amides combine a carbonyl group and nitrogen.

97927.e: Thiols are the sulphur analogues of alcohols. Many smell very strongly even in tiny amounts.

97928.q: Which functional group do nitriles have?
97928.e: Nitriles contain a carbon-nitrogen triple bond. One example is acetonitrile.

97929.q: Which of these groups has the highest priority for the name in IUPAC nomenclature?
97929.e: Carboxylic acids rank above aldehydes, ketones, alcohols and amines. Their group therefore determines the ending of the name.
97929.m: The carboxyl group takes priority in naming.

97930.q: Which two functional groups does lactic acid have?
97930.e: The IUPAC name of lactic acid is 2-hydroxypropanoic acid: “2-hydroxy” stands for the OH group and “-oic acid” for the COOH group. It is a hydroxycarboxylic acid.
97930.m: Lactic acid is a hydroxycarboxylic acid.

98129.e: Wheat is a cereal. Its grains are made into flour for bread.
98129.m: Wheat is the most important bread cereal.

98130.q: Which of these plants is a cereal?
98130.e: Barley is a cereal like wheat, rye and oats. Potato, carrot and pea are vegetables.
98130.m: Barley, rye and oats are cereals.

98131.q: What is a field where grain is grown called?
98131.e: An arable field is a field that is ploughed and planted. On a pasture, by contrast, animals eat grass.

98132.q: What was a flail used for in the past?
a: To beat grains out of the ears
98132.e: With the flail, people beat the ears lying on the floor. This knocked the grains out.
98132.m: In the past, grain was threshed with a flail.

98133.q: Which cereal is polenta cooked from?
98133.e: Polenta is a porridge made from maize semolina. It is especially popular in Ticino.

98134.q: What is left of the grain stalks after threshing?
98134.e: The dry stalks without grains are called straw. Farmers use it, for example, as bedding in the barn.
98134.m: Straw is the dry stalks of cereals.

98135.q: Which cereal is grown most in Switzerland?
98135.e: Wheat grows most on Swiss fields. It is mainly used to make bread.
98135.m: Wheat is grown most in Switzerland.

98136.q: From which part of a cereal grain does a new plant grow?
98136.e: The germ holds the tiny new plant. When the grain gets into damp soil, it starts to grow.
98136.m: The germ is the baby plant in the grain.

98137.q: What does a cereal grain need in the soil to sprout?
98137.e: A grain needs water and warmth to sprout. Then a root and a stalk grow.

98138.q: What is an ear of grain?
98138.e: The ear sits at the top of the grain stalk. The grains grow tightly packed inside it.
98138.m: The grains sit in the ear.

98139.q: What are the long bristles on some ears of grain called?
98139.e: Awns are long, thin bristles on the grains. They stick far out of the ear.
98139.m: The bristles on the ear are called awns.

98140.q: Which cereal has especially long awns?
98140.e: Because of its long awns, an ear of barley looks almost like a paintbrush.
98140.m: You can recognise barley by its long awns.

98141.q: Oats have no ear. What is their flower head called?
98141.e: In oats, the grains hang singly on fine little branches. This kind of flower head is called a panicle.
98141.m: Oats carry their grains in a panicle.

98142.q: What colour is a ripe ear of wheat?
98142.e: Young ears are green. When they are ripe and dry, they turn golden yellow.

98143.q: Which cereal plant carries its grains on a cob?
98143.e: In maize, the grains sit in rows on a thick cob. Wheat, barley and rye have ears.
98143.m: Maize kernels grow on a cob.

98144.q: Why do ripe ears of grain often hang down?
98144.e: When the grains are ripe and plump, the ear becomes heavy. That is why the stalk bends down.
98144.m: Full ears are heavy and droop.

98145.q: What are the grains in the ear for the plant?
98145.e: The grains are the seeds of the cereal. A new plant can grow from every grain.

98146.q: What is made from cereal grains in a mill?
98146.e: In the mill, the grains are ground finely. This makes flour.
98146.m: In the mill, grain is ground into flour.

98147.q: What is the job of someone who grinds grain called?
98147.e: The miller grinds the grain into flour in the mill. The baker then bakes bread from it.
98147.m: The miller grinds, the baker bakes.

98148.q: What used to turn a mill by a stream?
98148.e: The flowing water turned a big wheel. This wheel drove the millstones.
98148.m: A watermill uses the power of water.

98149.q: What is a mill with big sails that turn in the wind called?
98149.e: In a windmill, the wind blows into the sails. This turns the mill without electricity.
98149.m: A windmill is driven by the wind.

98150.q: What was used to grind the grain in old mills?
98150.e: Two heavy, round stones lay on top of each other. The upper one turned and ground the grains.
98150.m: In the past, heavy millstones ground the grain.

98151.q: What do modern mills mostly use to grind grain?
98151.e: Today the grains pass between smooth or grooved steel rollers. This is fast and very fine.
98151.m: Modern mills grind with steel rollers.

98152.q: What are the bits of husk left over from milling called?
98152.e: Bran is made of the outer layers of the grains. For white flour it is separated out.
98152.m: Bran is the ground outer layer of the grain.

98153.q: What does the mill do with the grain before grinding it?
98153.e: First, little stones, dust and other seeds are removed. Only then does the clean grain go for grinding.

98154.q: What is coarsely ground grain, for example for a pudding, called?
98154.e: Semolina is coarser than flour. It is used to cook semolina pudding with milk, for example.
98154.m: Semolina is ground more coarsely than flour.

98155.e: To make flour, cereal grains are ground, for example wheat or spelt.

98156.q: Why is white flour so pale?
a: The outer layer has been removed
98156.e: For white flour only the pale inside of the grain is used. The dark outer layer is separated out.
98156.m: White flour is pale because the outer layer is missing.

98157.q: In Switzerland, what is the dark flour used to bake Ruchbrot called?
98157.e: Ruchmehl contains more of the outer layer than white flour. That is why it is darker.
98157.m: The dark Ruchbrot is baked from Ruchmehl.

98158.q: Which flour is between white flour and Ruchmehl in colour?
98158.e: Half-white flour is a bit darker than white flour but paler than Ruchmehl. It is often used for bread.

98159.q: What is flour mainly made of?
98159.e: Flour consists mostly of starch. It gives the body energy.

98160.q: What is the best way to store flour?
98160.e: Damp flour can go mouldy. If it is well sealed, no small creatures can get in either.
98160.m: Flour must be stored dry and sealed.

98161.q: Which small creature likes to live in old flour supplies?
98161.e: The mealworm is the larva of a beetle. It eats flour and grain.

98162.q: What do you make in a frying pan from flour, eggs and milk?
98162.e: Flour, eggs and milk make a runny batter. It is cooked thinly in the pan.
98162.m: Pancakes are made from flour, eggs and milk.

98163.q: What happens when you stir a little flour into a sauce?
98163.e: When cooked, the starch in the flour binds the water. That is why the sauce gets thicker.

98164.e: For wholemeal flour the whole grain is ground, with its outer layer and germ.
98164.m: Wholemeal means the whole grain is in it.

98165.q: What does wholemeal bread do compared with white bread?
a: It keeps you full for longer
98165.e: The body digests the fibre in wholemeal slowly. That is why you stay full for longer.
98165.m: Wholemeal bread keeps you full for a long time.

98166.q: Where in the grain are there lots of vitamins and minerals?
a: In the outer layer and germ
98166.e: The outer layers and the germ are especially rich in vitamins. In wholemeal bread they are kept.
98166.m: The outer layer and germ are full of vitamins.

98167.q: How can you often recognise wholemeal bread?
a: By bits of husk in the bread
By a hole in the middle
98167.e: In wholemeal bread you often see small dark bits. These are pieces of the grain's outer layer.
98167.m: You can see bits of husk in wholemeal bread.

98168.q: Which bread does the Swiss food pyramid especially recommend?
98168.e: The food pyramid advises choosing wholemeal cereal products. They contain more valuable nutrients.

98169.q: What does yeast do in bread dough?
98169.e: Yeast forms small gas bubbles in the dough. This makes the dough bigger and lighter.

98170.q: What does the yeast produce in the dough that puffs it up?
98170.e: The yeast produces the gas carbon dioxide. It makes lots of small bubbles in the dough.
98170.m: The yeast's gas bubbles make the dough big.

98171.q: Where does a yeast dough rise best?
