99452.e: Each deeper layer is driven by the one above it and deflected further. The arrows of the current therefore turn in a spiral with depth.
99452.m: In the Ekman spiral the current turns with depth.

99453.q: How does the speed of the current in the Ekman spiral change with increasing depth?
a: It is greatest at the bottom
99453.e: Because of friction, each deeper layer loses momentum. Below the Ekman layer the wind-driven current has almost disappeared.
99453.m: The Ekman current gets weaker with depth.

99454.q: Why is the surface water of the sea not carried exactly in the direction of the wind?
a: The Earth's rotation deflects the moving water sideways
The water is attracted by the Moon
The salt slows the water down on one side
99454.e: The Coriolis force is caused by the Earth's rotation and deflects moving water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
99454.m: The Coriolis force deflects ocean currents away from the wind.

99455.q: Which polar explorer observed that drift ice did not drift exactly with the wind, which led to the Ekman theory?
99455.e: On the Fram expedition, Nansen noticed that the ice drifted to the right of the wind direction. Vagn Walfrid Ekman explained this mathematically in 1905.
99455.m: Nansen's observation of drift ice led to the Ekman theory.

99456.q: Why does floating plastic waste collect in the large subtropical ocean gyres?
a: Ekman transport carries the surface water towards the centre of the gyres
The water at the centre is free of salt
There is no Coriolis force there
99456.e: In the subtropical gyres, the winds drive the water towards the middle through Ekman transport. Floating objects build up there, for example in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.
99456.m: Ekman convergence collects floating debris in the middle of ocean gyres.

99457.q: What happens in the equatorial Pacific during an El Niño event?
a: The surface water in the central and eastern Pacific becomes unusually warm
The water off Peru becomes unusually cold
99457.e: During El Niño, warm water spreads east from the western Pacific. This changes air pressure, winds and rainfall worldwide.
99457.m: El Niño brings warm water to the eastern Pacific.

99458.q: Where does the name El Niño come from?
a: From Peruvian fishermen, because the warm water often appeared around Christmas
From a ship that discovered the effect
From an island in the Atlantic
99458.e: In Spanish, El Niño means “the boy” and refers to the Christ Child. The warming off the coast of Peru often appeared around Christmas time.
99458.m: El Niño is named after the Christ Child.

99459.q: What is the cool counterpart of El Niño called?
99459.e: During La Niña the trade winds are stronger and the water in the eastern Pacific is colder than normal. Together with El Niño, it forms the two extremes of the same climate phenomenon.
99459.m: La Niña is the cold phase of the ENSO phenomenon.

99460.q: What does the abbreviation ENSO stand for?
99460.e: ENSO links the ocean warming El Niño with the Southern Oscillation, a seesaw in air pressure between Tahiti and Darwin. Ocean and atmosphere are closely coupled.
99460.m: ENSO links ocean and atmosphere in the tropical Pacific.

99461.q: What happens to the trade winds over the equatorial Pacific during El Niño?
99461.e: Normally the trade winds push warm water westwards. When they weaken, the warm water sloshes back to the east.
99461.m: During El Niño the trade winds weaken.

99462.q: What effect does El Niño typically have on fishing off Peru?
99462.e: Warm surface water suppresses the upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water. As a result there is a lack of plankton, and the fish stocks off Peru decline sharply.
99462.m: El Niño weakens fishing off Peru.

99463.q: Roughly how often do El Niño events occur?
99463.e: El Niño is not strictly periodic; it occurs irregularly about every two to seven years. An event usually lasts nine to twelve months.
99463.m: El Niño returns irregularly every few years.

99464.q: How does the thermocline in the eastern equatorial Pacific change during El Niño?
99464.e: Because warm water collects in the east, the thermocline sinks there. Water that wells up then comes from the warm, nutrient-poor layer above.
99464.m: During El Niño the thermocline off South America is pushed down.

99465.q: Roughly what is the average salinity of seawater?
99465.e: One kilogram of seawater contains on average about 35 grams of dissolved salts. This is also written as 35 per mille or as a practical salinity of 35.
99465.m: Seawater contains on average about 3.5 per cent salt.

99466.q: Which ion makes up the largest share by mass of the dissolved salts in seawater?
99466.e: Chloride makes up about 55 per cent of the mass of dissolved salt, sodium about 30 per cent. Together they correspond to table salt.
99466.m: Chloride is the most common ion in seawater.

99467.q: Which marginal sea is especially salty, with values around 40 grams per kilogram, because of strong evaporation and little inflow?
99467.e: A lot of water evaporates in the Red Sea, and hardly any rivers flow into it. That is why it is one of the saltiest seas with open access to the ocean.
99467.m: The Red Sea is especially salty.

99468.q: Why is the Baltic Sea a brackish sea with low salinity?
a: Many rivers bring fresh water, and exchange with the North Sea is small
Because sea ice melts there every day
Because it is deeper than the Atlantic
99468.e: The Baltic Sea receives a lot of fresh water from rivers and precipitation. Salty North Sea water only gets in through the narrow Danish straits.
99468.m: Plenty of fresh water and little exchange make the Baltic brackish.

99469.q: How is salinity in the sea usually measured today?
a: Through the electrical conductivity of the water
Through the cloudiness of the water
Through the colour of the water
Through the pH of the water
99469.e: Dissolved ions conduct electricity: the more salt, the higher the conductivity. The 1978 Practical Salinity Scale is based on this relationship, corrected for temperature and pressure.

99470.q: Why is seawater denser than fresh water?
a: Because salts are dissolved in it
Because it is always colder than fresh water
Because it contains more air bubbles
Because it is coloured green by algae
99470.e: The dissolved salts increase the mass per volume. That is why it is easier to float in the sea than in a lake.

99471.q: What does the principle of constant proportions state for seawater?
a: The ratios of the main ions are almost the same everywhere
Every ocean has exactly the same salinity
The salt content always increases with depth
Salt and water evaporate at the same rate
99471.e: Even if the total salt content varies, the ratios of, for example, chloride, sodium and sulphate stay constant. That is why the total salinity can be worked out from one component.
99471.m: The main ions in seawater are in fixed ratios to each other.

99472.q: What happens to the salinity of the surrounding water when sea ice forms?
a: It rises, because most of the salt is pushed out during freezing
The water turns into fresh water
99472.e: Ice crystals take in hardly any salt, and the brine goes into the water below. This becomes heavier and sinks, which helps to form deep water.
99472.m: When sea ice forms, the water below becomes saltier and heavier.

99473.q: Why is surface salinity especially high in the subtropics?
a: More water evaporates there than falls as precipitation
The largest rivers flow into the sea there
99473.e: In the subtropical high-pressure areas it is dry and sunny. The strong evaporation concentrates the salt at the surface.
99473.m: High evaporation raises the salt content at the sea surface.

99474.q: What happens in an upwelling area in the ocean?
a: Cold, nutrient-rich deep water rises to the surface
Warm surface water sinks into the deep sea
Fresh water flows up from the seabed
99474.e: In upwelling, water from the depths replaces surface water that has been carried away. It brings nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate into the light.
99474.m: In upwelling areas, nutrient-rich deep water comes to the top.

99475.q: On which coasts are the large coastal upwelling areas typically found?
a: On the west coasts of the continents at low latitudes
On the east coasts in the polar regions
Only on islands in the Indian Ocean
99475.e: Examples are the coasts off Peru and Chile, Namibia, California and north-west Africa. There, winds blow parallel to the coast towards the equator.
99475.m: Large upwelling areas lie on the west coasts of the continents.

99476.q: Why do winds along the coast cause upwelling off Peru?
a: Ekman transport carries surface water away from the coast
The wind pushes water towards the coast
The tides pump water up from the depths
99476.e: Winds blowing parallel to the coast towards the equator carry the surface water out to the open sea through Ekman transport. Cold deep water flows in from below to replace it.
99476.m: Offshore Ekman transport creates coastal upwelling.

99477.q: Why are upwelling areas so important for fishing?
a: The nutrients make a great deal of plankton grow
The water there is especially warm
There are no predatory fish there
The water there is free of salt
99477.e: Plankton forms the basis of a rich food chain. Although upwelling areas make up only a small part of the sea's surface, a large part of the world's fish catch comes from there.
99477.m: Upwelling areas are among the most productive regions of the sea.

99478.q: Which fish species is caught in especially large quantities in the upwelling area of the Humboldt Current?
99478.e: The Peruvian anchovy (anchoveta) forms huge shoals in the cold, nutrient-rich water off Peru. It is mainly processed into fishmeal and fish oil.
99478.m: The anchoveta lives on the plankton of the Humboldt upwelling.

99479.q: Why is there upwelling at the equator in the Pacific?
a: Ekman transport carries water away to the north and south of the equator
The Coriolis force is strongest at the equator
The sea is shallowest at the equator
Most rivers flow into the sea there
99479.e: The trade winds blow westwards on both sides of the equator. Ekman transport deflects the surface water towards the poles on both sides, and this divergence sucks deep water up.
99479.m: At the equator the Ekman transports move apart and cause upwelling.

99480.q: Why are there often deserts such as the Atacama or the Namib on coasts with strong upwelling?
a: Cold upwelling water cools the lower air and stabilises it, so hardly any rain falls
The sea releases salt into the air there, which prevents rain
99480.e: Over cold water, a stable layering of air with an inversion forms. Moist air can hardly rise, so no rain clouds form.
99480.m: Cold upwelling water encourages coastal deserts.

99481.q: Which weather phenomenon is especially common on coasts with cold upwelling water?
99481.e: When moist sea air cools over cold water, it condenses into fog. In Chile this fog is called camanchaca and is partly harvested with fog nets.
99481.m: Coastal fog often forms over cold upwelling water.

99482.q: At which plate boundaries do deep-sea trenches form?
a: At hotspots in the middle of a plate
At transform faults with no movement
99482.e: A deep-sea trench forms where one oceanic plate sinks beneath another. Volcanic arcs and strong earthquakes nearby are typical.
99482.m: Deep-sea trenches mark zones where a plate sinks.

99483.q: Which deep-sea trench contains the deepest known point in the oceans?
99483.e: In the Challenger Deep of the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific, almost 11,000 m has been measured. No other place in the sea is deeper.
99483.m: The Mariana Trench is the deepest trench on Earth.

99484.q: Which Swiss man reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench together with Don Walsh in 1960?
99484.e: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh dived into the Challenger Deep in the submersible Trieste on 23 January 1960. It was the first visit by people to the deepest point of the sea.
99484.m: In 1960 Jacques Piccard was the first to dive to the deepest point of the sea.

99485.q: Who designed the deep-sea submersible Trieste, with which the Mariana Trench was reached?
99485.e: The Swiss physicist Auguste Piccard developed the principle of the bathyscaphe. The Trieste was built in Italy in 1953 and later taken over by the US Navy.
99485.m: Auguste Piccard built the bathyscaphe Trieste.

99486.q: From what depth does the hadal zone begin, which occurs almost only in deep-sea trenches?
99486.e: The hadal zone is named after the Greek Hades. It includes the deepest areas of the ocean below the abyssal plains.
99486.m: The hadal zone begins at a depth of about 6000 m.

99487.q: Roughly how high is the water pressure at the bottom of the Mariana Trench if it increases by about 1 bar for every 10 m of depth?
99487.e: Almost 11,000 m divided by 10 m gives about 1100 bar. That is over a thousand times more than the air pressure at the sea surface.
99487.m: At the deepest point of the sea the pressure is over 1000 bar.

99488.q: Who was the first person to dive alone to the bottom of the Challenger Deep, in 2012?
99488.e: The film director James Cameron reached the Challenger Deep on 26 March 2012 in the submersible Deepsea Challenger. This made him the first solo diver at this spot.
99488.m: In 2012 James Cameron dived alone into the Mariana Trench.

99490.q: In which deep-sea trench is the deepest point of the Atlantic Ocean?
99490.e: The Puerto Rico Trench reaches a depth of about 8400 m. It lies on the boundary between the Caribbean and North American Plates.
99490.m: The deepest point of the Atlantic is in the Puerto Rico Trench.

99790.q: How many proteinogenic amino acids are coded directly by the standard genetic code?
99790.e: The standard code encodes 20 amino acids. Selenocysteine and pyrrolysine are only built in through special mechanisms.
99790.m: The genetic code encodes 20 standard amino acids.

99791.q: Which two functional groups does every amino acid have?
99791.e: The name gives it away: a basic amino group and an acidic carboxyl group. In proteinogenic amino acids, both are on the same carbon atom.
99791.m: Every amino acid carries an amino group and a carboxyl group.

99792.q: Which messenger substance does the body make from the amino acid tryptophan?
99792.e: Tryptophan is an essential amino acid. The body uses it to build the messenger serotonin and later the sleep hormone melatonin.
99792.m: The body makes serotonin from tryptophan.

99793.q: What are amino acids called whose side chain is positively charged at neutral pH?
99793.e: Lysine and arginine carry an extra nitrogen-containing group in their side chain. It takes up a proton and is then positively charged.
99793.m: Lysine is a basic amino acid.

99794.q: Which reagent is used to make amino acids visible, for example on chromatography plates or in fingerprints?
99794.e: Ninhydrin reacts with the amino group of free amino acids to form a bluish-purple dye. Forensic science uses this for fingerprints on paper.

99795.q: What does the isoelectric point of an amino acid describe?
a: The pH at which its net charge is zero
The temperature at which it melts
The pH at which it is fully protonated
The voltage at which it decomposes
99795.e: At the isoelectric point, the amino acid does not move in an electric field. Its solubility in water is also usually lowest there.
99795.m: At the isoelectric point, an amino acid has no overall charge.

99796.q: What does the term “essential amino acid” mean?
a: The body cannot make it itself
It is poisonous to the body
It is only made in plants
99796.e: Essential amino acids such as leucine or lysine must be taken in with food. The body can make others itself from precursors.
99796.m: Essential amino acids must come from food.

99797.q: Which proteinogenic amino acid can form disulphide bridges through its side chain?
99797.e: Cysteine carries a thiol group. Two cysteines can form a disulphide bridge by oxidation, which stabilises the three-dimensional structure of proteins.
99797.m: Cysteine links protein chains through sulphur bridges.

99798.q: What is the bond called that links two amino acids in a protein chain?
99798.e: The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the other and water is split off. This forms a peptide bond.
99798.m: Amino acids join through peptide bonds to form proteins.

99799.q: Which type of reaction forms a peptide bond?
99799.e: The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the next. A water molecule is released.
99799.m: Water is split off when a peptide bond forms.

99800.q: Which atoms does a peptide bond link directly?
a: The carbonyl carbon of one amino acid and the nitrogen of the other
Two sulphur atoms of two side chains
Two alpha carbon atoms directly to each other
The oxygen of one amino acid and the nitrogen of the other
99800.e: The peptide bond is an amide bond between the C atom of the former carboxyl group and the N atom of the amino group.
99800.m: The peptide bond is an amide bond between carbon and nitrogen.

99801.q: Why can the peptide bond not rotate freely?
a: Resonance gives it partial double bond character
It is a true triple bond
The side chains always get tangled
99801.e: The lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen is delocalised with the C=O group. The atoms of the peptide group therefore lie in one plane.
99801.m: The peptide group is rigid and planar.

99802.q: How many water molecules are released when 100 amino acids form a linear chain?
99802.e: Between the 100 links of a chain there are 99 connections. Each peptide bond releases one water molecule.
99802.m: A chain of n amino acids has n minus 1 peptide bonds.

99803.q: How are the peptide bonds of proteins split during digestion?
a: By hydrolysis with the help of enzymes
99803.e: Digestive enzymes such as pepsin split peptide bonds by taking up water. This produces individual amino acids again.
99803.m: During digestion, peptide bonds are split by hydrolysis.

99804.q: Where in the cell are the peptide bonds of proteins formed?
99804.e: Ribosomes read the mRNA and link the amino acids in the right order. The catalysis is carried out by the ribosomal RNA.
99804.m: Ribosomes are the protein factories of the cell.

99805.q: Which level of protein structure is described by the sequence of amino acids linked by peptide bonds?
99805.e: The primary structure is the amino acid sequence. The alpha helix and the beta sheet belong to the secondary structure.
99805.m: The order of the amino acids is the primary structure.

99806.q: Which test reaction shows peptide bonds with a purple colour?
99806.e: In alkaline solution, copper(II) ions form a purple complex with at least two peptide bonds. This can be used to detect proteins.
99806.m: The biuret test turns proteins purple.

99807.q: What does an enzyme do in a chemical reaction?
a: It changes the enthalpy of reaction
It shifts the equilibrium towards the products
It raises the temperature of the solution
99807.e: Enzymes are biocatalysts. They speed up the forward and reverse reactions equally but change neither the enthalpy nor the position of equilibrium.
99807.m: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy.

99808.q: Who compared the binding of enzyme and substrate to a lock and key in 1894?
99808.e: Emil Fischer observed that enzymes only split certain sugar isomers. From this he came up with the image of a matching key.
99808.m: The lock and key model comes from Emil Fischer.

99809.q: What does the induced fit model describe?
a: The active site adjusts its shape when the substrate binds
The enzyme completely encloses and stores the substrate
An enzyme can bind any substrate at all
The enzyme is used up in the reaction
99809.e: In 1958 Daniel Koshland suggested that enzymes are flexible. Only the binding of the substrate brings the active site into its best shape.
99809.m: In induced fit, the enzyme shapes itself around its substrate.

99810.q: What does the Michaelis constant of an enzyme tell you?
a: The substrate concentration at half the maximum rate
The number of active sites per enzyme
The temperature at which the enzyme denatures
99810.e: A small Km value means that the enzyme is half saturated even at a low substrate concentration. This points to a high affinity.
99810.m: A small Michaelis constant shows a high affinity for the substrate.

99811.q: How can you recognise competitive inhibition?
a: It can be overcome with more substrate
The inhibitor only binds far from the active site
It only occurs at high temperatures
99811.e: The inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site. With a great deal of substrate, the maximum rate is still reached.
99811.m: In competitive inhibition, inhibitor and substrate compete for the same place.

99812.q: Why does enzyme activity fall sharply when the temperature rises well above the optimum?
a: The enzyme denatures and loses its three-dimensional structure
The enzyme is broken down into sugar
99812.e: Heat breaks hydrogen bonds and other weak bonds that hold the folding in place. The active site loses its shape.
99812.m: Too much heat destroys the shape of an enzyme.

99813.q: Which ending do the names of most enzymes have?
99813.e: Examples are amylase, protease and polymerase. Older names such as pepsin or trypsin do not follow this rule yet.

99814.q: In 1897 Eduard Buchner showed that even cell-free pressed yeast juice can ferment sugar. What followed from this?
a: Fermentation does not need living cells, but enzymes.
Yeast is made entirely of sugar.
Fermentation is only possible with oxygen.
Bacteria are absolutely necessary for fermentation.
99814.e: There were no living cells left in the pressed juice, yet fermentation still took place. So enzymes cause the reaction. Buchner received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this in 1907.
99814.m: Fermentation works without living cells because enzymes cause it.

99815.q: Where does the name “carbohydrates” come from?
a: Many have the formula Cn(H2O)m, as if they were hydrates of carbon
They form when coal is burnt
They always contain carbon and hydrogen but no oxygen
They were first discovered in coal mines
99815.e: Glucose, for example, can be written as C6(H2O)6. Chemically, however, carbohydrates do not contain water molecules but hydroxyl and carbonyl groups.
99815.m: Carbohydrates are named after their typical molecular formula.

99816.q: Which polysaccharide forms the exoskeleton of insects and crustaceans?
99816.e: Chitin is built from N-acetylglucosamine and therefore contains nitrogen. After cellulose, it is one of the most common biopolymers.

99817.q: How does cellulose differ chemically from the amylose in starch?
a: Its glucose units are linked by beta-1,4 instead of alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds
It is made of fructose instead of glucose
99817.e: The beta linkage produces long, straight chains that bundle into strong fibres. Humans lack the enzymes to split this bond.
99817.m: Cellulose and starch differ only in the type of glycosidic bond.

99818.q: Which group of monosaccharides does fructose belong to?
99818.e: Fructose has six C atoms and a keto group on the second carbon. Glucose, on the other hand, is an aldohexose.
99818.m: Fructose is a sugar with six C atoms and a keto group.

99819.q: How does amylopectin differ from amylose?
a: It is branched by extra alpha-1,6 bonds
It is made of fructose instead of glucose
99819.e: Amylose is an unbranched chain that coils into a helix. Amylopectin has a branch roughly every 20 to 30 glucose units.
99819.m: Amylopectin is the branched form of starch.

99820.q: What does a brick-red precipitate in Fehling's test show?
99820.e: Reducing sugars such as glucose reduce copper(II) ions to red copper(I) oxide. Sucrose does not give a positive test.

99821.q: Which ring form does glucose mainly take in aqueous solution?
99821.e: The hydroxyl group on the fifth C atom reacts with the aldehyde group to form a hemiacetal. This produces a six-membered ring containing an oxygen atom.
99821.m: In solution, glucose is mostly a six-membered ring.

99822.q: What are the two ring forms of glucose called, which differ only in the position of the OH group on the C1 atom?
99822.e: When the ring closes, the OH group on C1 can point down or up. Starch is made from alpha glucose, cellulose from beta glucose.
99822.m: When its ring closes, glucose forms an alpha and a beta form.

99823.q: Which property do all lipids have in common?
a: They dissolve poorly in water but well in non-polar solvents
They are all made of amino acids
They are all solid at room temperature
99823.e: Lipids are defined by their solubility, not by a shared structure. They include fats, waxes, steroids and phospholipids.
99823.m: Lipids are the water-repelling substances of the cell.

99824.q: Which enzyme breaks down dietary fats in the small intestine?
99824.e: Lipase from the pancreas splits fatty acids off glycerol. Bile acids help by breaking the fat into small droplets.

99825.q: Which structure do phospholipids form on their own in water?
99825.e: The polar heads face the water and the non-polar tails face each other. This forms bilayers, the basis of all cell membranes.
99825.m: Phospholipids form the bilayer of the cell membrane.

99826.q: What are molecules such as phospholipids with a water-loving head and a water-repelling tail called?
99826.e: Amphiphilic substances combine polar and non-polar regions in one molecule. Soaps and surfactants are amphiphilic too.
99826.m: Amphiphilic molecules like water and fat at the same time.

99827.q: Which group of lipids does cholesterol belong to?
99827.e: Cholesterol has the typical framework of four joined carbon rings. The body uses it to make steroid hormones and bile acids.

99828.q: Roughly what is the energy value of fat?
99828.e: Fat provides about 9 kcal or 37 kJ per gram, more than twice as much as carbohydrates or proteins with about 17 kJ per gram each.
99828.m: Fat is the most energy-rich nutrient.

99829.q: Which lipoproteins carry cholesterol from the liver to the body's tissues?
99829.e: Low-density lipoproteins bring cholesterol to the cells. HDL, on the other hand, carries surplus cholesterol back to the liver.
99829.m: LDL brings cholesterol to the tissues.

99830.q: How are liquid vegetable oils made solid when fats are hardened?
a: By catalytic hydrogenation of the double bonds
By oxidation with oxygen from the air
99830.e: Hydrogen is added to the C=C double bonds with nickel as a catalyst. If hardening is incomplete, trans fatty acids can form.
99830.m: When fats are hardened, double bonds are saturated with hydrogen.

99831.q: What characterises a saturated fatty acid?
a: It contains no C=C double bonds
It is completely dissolved in water
It contains at least three double bonds
It has a branched chain with a ring
99831.e: In saturated fatty acids, every C atom in the chain carries the maximum number of hydrogen atoms. Examples are palmitic acid and stearic acid.
99831.m: Saturated fatty acids have only single bonds.

99832.q: How many C=C double bonds does oleic acid have?
99832.e: Oleic acid is a monounsaturated fatty acid with 18 C atoms and one cis double bond. It is the main component of olive oil.

99833.q: How many carbon atoms does saturated palmitic acid have?
99833.e: Palmitic acid is hexadecanoic acid with 16 C atoms. Its name comes from palm oil.

99834.q: What does the term “omega-3 fatty acid” mean?
a: The first double bond is at the third C atom from the end of the chain
The fatty acid has exactly three double bonds
The fatty acid consists of three chains
The fatty acid has three carboxyl groups
99834.e: Omega refers to the last C atom of the chain, the methyl end. You count from there to the first double bond.
99834.m: Omega-3 tells you where the first double bond is, counting from the end of the chain.

99835.q: Why are fats with many unsaturated fatty acids usually liquid at room temperature?
a: cis double bonds bend the chains so they pack less tightly
Unsaturated fatty acids form more hydrogen bonds
99835.e: Straight chains lie close together and form many van der Waals contacts. Bent chains do this less, so the melting point falls.
99835.m: Bent fatty acid chains lower the melting point.

99836.q: Why has Switzerland limited the content of trans fatty acids in edible fats since 2008?
a: They increase the risk of heart and circulatory diseases.
They make fats go rancid faster.
99836.e: Trans fatty acids raise harmful LDL cholesterol in the blood. Switzerland was one of the first countries after Denmark to introduce a limit.
99836.m: Trans fats harm the heart and blood vessels.

99837.q: Which fatty acid is essential for humans?
99837.e: Humans cannot introduce double bonds beyond the ninth C atom. The omega-6 fatty acid linoleic acid must therefore come from food.
99837.m: Linoleic acid must be taken in with food.

99838.q: What is the pathway called that breaks down fatty acids in the mitochondria?
99838.e: In each round, a piece with two C atoms is split off as acetyl-CoA. This is broken down further in the citric acid cycle.
99838.m: Fatty acids are broken down two carbons at a time.

99839.q: What building blocks are nucleic acids made of?
99839.e: Nucleic acids are polymers made of many nucleotides in a row. They store and pass on genetic information.
99839.m: Nucleic acids are chains of nucleotides.

99840.q: Which three parts make up a nucleotide?
a: Amino group, carboxyl group and side chain
99840.e: The base is attached to C1 of the sugar and the phosphate group to C5. The nucleotides link into a chain through the phosphates.
99840.m: A nucleotide consists of phosphate, sugar and base.

99841.q: Which base is found in RNA instead of thymine?
99841.e: Like thymine, uracil pairs with adenine but has no methyl group. DNA uses thymine.

99842.q: Which doctor from Basel discovered nucleic acids in 1869, calling them “nuclein”?
99842.e: In Tübingen, Friedrich Miescher isolated a phosphorus-rich substance from the nuclei of white blood cells. He later taught at the University of Basel.
99842.m: Friedrich Miescher from Basel discovered nucleic acids.

99843.e: Purines consist of two joined rings. Cytosine, thymine and uracil are single-ring pyrimidines.
99843.m: Adenine and guanine are the purine bases.

99844.q: Which bond links the nucleotides in the backbone of a nucleic acid?
99844.e: A phosphate group links C3 of one sugar with C5 of the next. This creates a backbone of sugar and phosphate.
99844.m: Phosphodiester bonds form the backbone of DNA and RNA.

99845.q: What is the job of messenger RNA (mRNA)?
a: It carries the information of a gene to the ribosomes
It permanently stores the entire genome
It brings amino acids to the ribosome
99845.e: The mRNA is a copy of a gene. At the ribosome, its base sequence is translated into a chain of amino acids.
99845.m: The mRNA brings the blueprint of a protein to the ribosome.

a: RNA molecules that catalyse chemical reactions
99846.e: Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman discovered catalytically active RNA in the 1980s. This supports the idea of an early “RNA world”.
99846.m: RNA can not only carry information but also act as a catalyst.

99847.q: Whose X-ray diffraction image “Photo 51” was crucial for working out the structure of DNA?
99847.e: Rosalind Franklin and her doctoral student Raymond Gosling took the image in 1952. The cross-shaped pattern revealed the helix shape.
99847.m: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray image helped reveal the double helix.

99848.q: Which base does guanine pair with in DNA?
99848.e: In the double helix, a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine. Guanine binds to cytosine, adenine to thymine.

99849.q: How many hydrogen bonds do guanine and cytosine form with each other?
99849.e: G-C pairs have three hydrogen bonds, A-T pairs two. DNA with a high GC content is therefore more stable when heated.
99849.m: A G-C pair is held together by three hydrogen bonds.

99850.q: A double-stranded DNA contains 30 per cent adenine. What is its share of guanine?
99850.e: According to Chargaff's rule, thymine is also 30 per cent. That leaves 40 per cent for guanine and cytosine, so 20 per cent each.
99850.m: Adenine and thymine, and guanine and cytosine, occur in equal amounts.

99851.q: How are the two strands of the DNA double helix oriented to each other?
99851.e: One strand runs from the 5' end to the 3' end, the other strand in the opposite direction. Only this way do the base pairs fit together geometrically.
99851.m: The DNA strands run in opposite directions.

99852.q: How does deoxyribose differ from the sugar in RNA?
a: It lacks a hydroxyl group on the second C atom
It has two more carbon atoms
It contains a nitrogen atom in the ring
It is a six-membered ring instead of a five-membered one
99852.e: “Deoxy” means “without oxygen”. The missing 2'-OH group makes DNA chemically more stable than RNA.
99852.m: Deoxyribose lacks an oxygen atom on the second carbon.

99853.q: What does “semi-conservative replication” of DNA mean?
a: Each new double helix contains one old and one new strand
The old double helix stays complete, the new one is entirely new
Old and new pieces are mixed randomly
Only half of the genes are copied
99853.e: Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl proved this in 1958 using heavy nitrogen isotopes. Each parent strand serves as a template for a new strand.
99853.m: In replication, each daughter DNA keeps one old strand.

99854.q: Roughly how many base pairs make up the single human genome?
99854.e: The haploid human genome has about 3.1 billion base pairs. Only a small part of it codes for proteins.
99854.m: The human genome has about three billion base pairs.

99855.q: What are the components of ATP?
a: Adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups
Adenine, deoxyribose and one phosphate group
Adenine, glucose and two phosphate groups
Guanine, ribose and three phosphate groups
99855.e: ATP is a nucleotide. The three phosphate groups hang in a row on the C5 atom of the ribose.
99855.m: ATP consists of adenine, ribose and three phosphates.

99856.q: Under standard conditions, how much energy is released when ATP is hydrolysed to ADP?
99856.e: The standard value is about minus 30.5 kJ/mol. Under the conditions inside the cell it is even about 50 kJ/mol.
99856.m: Splitting ATP provides energy in portions.

99857.q: In which cell organelles is most of the ATP made during cellular respiration?
99857.e: The respiratory chain and ATP synthesis take place in the inner mitochondrial membrane. That is why mitochondria are also called the powerhouses of the cell.
99857.m: Mitochondria are the powerhouses of the cell.

99858.q: What drives ATP synthase in the inner mitochondrial membrane?
a: A proton gradient across the membrane
The splitting of glucose inside the enzyme itself
A sodium gradient in the nucleus
99858.e: The respiratory chain pumps protons outwards. They flow back through ATP synthase and drive it like a turbine. Peter Mitchell received the Nobel Prize for this in 1978.
99858.m: A flow of protons drives ATP synthase.

99859.q: What is the job of ATP in the cell?
a: It serves as a universal energy carrier
It carries oxygen in the blood
99859.e: Energy is released when a phosphate group is split off. The cell uses this to power muscle movement, transport and synthesis, for example.
99859.m: ATP is the energy currency of the cell.

99860.q: How much ATP does glycolysis gain overall from one molecule of glucose?
99860.e: In glycolysis, 2 ATP are invested and 4 ATP are made. The net gain is 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
99860.m: Glycolysis gives a net gain of two ATP per glucose.

99861.q: Roughly how much ATP does a person turn over per day?
a: about as much as their own body weight
about ten times their body weight
99861.e: The body contains only a few tens of grams of ATP. But each molecule is split and remade thousands of times a day.
99861.m: ATP is constantly used up and rebuilt.

99862.q: Which molecule forms when two phosphate groups are split off ATP?
99862.e: Adenosine monophosphate carries only one phosphate. In many syntheses, the cell splits ATP directly into AMP and pyrophosphate.
99862.m: Splitting two phosphates off ATP gives AMP.

99863.e: Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed together with fat and stored in the body. The B vitamins and vitamin C are water-soluble.
99863.m: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble.

99864.q: Which disease is caused by a lack of vitamin C?
99864.e: Without vitamin C, the body cannot make stable collagen. Bleeding gums and wounds that heal badly used to be common among sailors.
99864.m: A lack of vitamin C leads to scurvy.

99865.q: How does the body make vitamin D itself?
a: Through UVB radiation on the skin
99865.e: In the skin, 7-dehydrocholesterol, a precursor of cholesterol, is converted by UVB light. In winter, the sun in Switzerland is often not strong enough for this.
99865.m: Sunlight helps the skin make vitamin D.

99866.q: Where does the word “vitamin” come from?
a: From the name of a researcher called Vitam
99866.e: In 1912 the biochemist Casimir Funk called these substances “vital amines” because he suspected they were vital nitrogen-containing compounds. It later turned out that not all vitamins are amines.
99866.m: The word vitamin comes from “vital amine”.

99867.q: Which metal atom does vitamin B12 contain?
99867.e: Vitamin B12 is also called cobalamin. The cobalt sits in the centre of a ring system, similar to iron in haem.
99867.m: Vitamin B12 is the only vitamin containing cobalt.

99868.q: What does the body mainly need vitamin K for?
99868.e: Vitamin K is needed to activate several clotting factors in the liver. The K comes from the German word “Koagulation”, meaning coagulation.
99868.m: Vitamin K helps the blood to clot.

99869.q: Which disease results from a lack of vitamin B1 (thiamine)?
99869.e: Beriberi was especially common among people who ate mainly polished rice. Thiamine is important for carbohydrate metabolism and the nerves.
99869.m: A lack of thiamine causes beriberi.

99870.q: Which early symptom does a lack of vitamin A show?
99870.e: Vitamin A is used to make retinal, the pigment in the rods of the retina. Without it, you see poorly in dim light.
99870.m: Vitamin A is important for seeing in the dark.

99871.q: For which vitamin did Tadeus Reichstein develop a synthesis suitable for industry in the early 1930s?
99871.e: The Reichstein process makes ascorbic acid from glucose. Hoffmann-La Roche in Basel used it to produce vitamin C in large quantities.
99871.m: The Reichstein process made vitamin C cheap.

99872.q: In which category did Tadeus Reichstein receive the Nobel Prize in 1950?
99872.e: Reichstein shared the prize with the Americans Edward Kendall and Philip Hench. He is one of the few chemists with a Nobel Prize in Medicine.
99872.m: Reichstein received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.

99873.q: For which discoveries was Tadeus Reichstein awarded the Nobel Prize?
a: On the hormones of the adrenal cortex
99873.e: Reichstein isolated and studied numerous steroids from the adrenal cortex. These include cortisone.
99873.m: Reichstein researched the hormones of the adrenal cortex.

99874.q: From which sugar is vitamin C made in the Reichstein process?
99874.e: The Reichstein process starts with glucose, which is converted via sorbitol and sorbose into ascorbic acid. This is how vitamin C was produced industrially from the 1930s.
99874.m: The Reichstein process turns glucose into vitamin C.

99875.q: Which class of compounds do the hormones of the adrenal cortex such as cortisone, which Reichstein studied, belong to?
99875.e: Steroids have a basic framework of four joined carbon rings. Cholesterol also belongs to this class of compounds.

99876.q: Which Basel company produced vitamin C in large quantities using Tadeus Reichstein's process?
99876.e: Roche bought the rights to the Reichstein process and became one of the world's largest vitamin producers. The process was used for decades.
99876.m: Roche made vitamin C using Reichstein's process.

99877.q: For which diseases did the adrenal cortex hormone cortisone prove particularly effective?
99877.e: Philip Hench first used cortisone for rheumatoid arthritis in 1948. Its anti-inflammatory effect was spectacular.

99878.q: Why are bacteria used for one step of the Reichstein process?
a: They oxidise only one specific part of the molecule
They supply the heat needed for the reaction
They colour the vitamin C yellow
They remove the water from the solution
99878.e: Acetic acid bacteria oxidise sorbitol at exactly one position to form sorbose. This targeted reaction would be hard to achieve chemically.
99878.m: The Reichstein process combines chemistry and microbiology.

99879.q: What did Paul Karrer receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for in 1937?
a: For research on carotenoids, flavins and vitamins A and B2
For the synthesis of vitamin C
For working out the structure of insulin
99879.e: Karrer worked out the structure of many natural pigments and vitamins. He shared the prize with the Briton Walter Haworth.
99879.m: Paul Karrer researched plant pigments and vitamins.

99880.q: Which orange plant pigment researched by Paul Karrer is a precursor of vitamin A?
99880.e: Karrer showed that the body can make vitamin A from beta-carotene, for example from carrots. Chlorophyll is green, anthocyanins are red to blue.
99880.m: The body makes vitamin A from beta-carotene.

99881.q: In which Swiss city did the Nobel Prize winner Paul Karrer teach and do research for about 40 years?
99881.e: Karrer headed the Chemical Institute of the University of Zurich from 1919 to 1959. He is one of this university's Nobel Prize winners.
99881.m: Paul Karrer did his research in Zurich.

99882.q: Which vitamin's structure did Paul Karrer become the first to work out in 1931?
99882.e: Karrer determined the structure of retinol and showed that it is related to beta-carotene. It was the first time the structure of a vitamin had been worked out.
99882.m: Karrer was the first to work out the structure of a vitamin.

99883.q: Which vitamin, also called tocopherol, did Paul Karrer synthesise in 1938?
99883.e: Karrer worked out the structure of alpha-tocopherol and synthesised it. Vitamin E protects cell membranes from oxidation.

99884.q: By which chemical name is vitamin B2, researched by Karrer, known?
99884.e: Vitamin B2 is called riboflavin and is one of the flavins. Thiamine is vitamin B1, cobalamin is B12 and ascorbic acid is vitamin C.

99885.q: Which deficiency symptom can occur with too little vitamin A, which Karrer researched?
99885.e: Vitamin A is needed for the visual pigment in the retina. Scurvy comes from a lack of vitamin C, rickets from a lack of vitamin D and beriberi from a lack of vitamin B1.
99885.m: Vitamin A is important for seeing in the dark.

99886.q: Which property do vitamins A and E, researched by Karrer, have in common?
a: They are made of amino acids
99886.e: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and are absorbed with fat from food. The B vitamins and vitamin C are water-soluble.
99886.m: Vitamins A and E are fat-soluble vitamins.

99887.q: What does a honeybee usually do on a collecting flight?
a: It visits only one kind of flower.
It changes kind at every flower.
99887.e: On one flight, honeybees usually stick to one kind of flower. That way the pollen reaches the right plant.
99887.m: A collecting bee usually sticks to one kind of flower.

99888.q: What is another word for the fine flower dust?
99888.e: The fine dust in flowers is called pollen. It is made of lots of tiny grains.

99889.q: Which garden vegetable needs insects to form fruit?
99889.e: Pumpkin flowers are pollinated by bees and bumblebees. Only then does a pumpkin grow.

99890.q: Which creatures pollinate many flowers at night in our part of the world?
99890.e: When the bees are asleep, moths are out and about. They visit flowers and carry pollen on.

99891.q: Why do fruit growers put bee colonies in their orchards in spring?
99891.e: The bees fly from tree to tree and pollinate the blossoms. That way there is more fruit in autumn.
99891.m: Bees in the orchard make for a good harvest.

99892.q: Why do cherry trees blossom before they bear cherries?
99892.e: The cherries later grow from pollinated cherry blossoms. That is why the blossom comes first.
99892.m: Without blossoms there are no cherries.

99893.q: Where does pollen get stuck on a bee?
a: on the tips of its feelers
99893.e: Bees are covered in fine hairs. Lots of pollen grains stick to them.
99893.m: Pollen sticks to the bees' hairs.

99894.q: Which part of the flower takes up the pollen?
99894.e: The stigma is sticky. The pollen gets stuck there, and the flower is pollinated.
99894.m: The sticky stigma catches the pollen.

99895.q: Why are there often fewer cherries after a rainy spring?
a: Bees hardly fly in the rain.
No leaves grow in the rain.
99895.e: Bees have to fly while the cherry trees are in blossom. In rain and cold they stay in the hive, and many blossoms are not pollinated.
99895.m: Rain during blossom time can make the harvest smaller.

99896.q: What is the mother of all the bees in a colony called?
99896.e: Every bee colony has a queen. She lays all the eggs.
99896.m: The queen lays the eggs in the bee colony.

99897.q: What are the female bees that collect nectar called?
99897.e: The workers collect nectar and pollen, build honeycomb and look after the young.
99897.m: The workers do almost all the jobs in the bee colony.

99898.e: Male bees are called drones. They have no sting and do not collect nectar.

99899.q: How do bees show other bees the way to flowers?
99899.e: A collecting bee dances on the honeycomb in the hive. This tells the others the direction and distance of the flowers.
99899.m: Bees reveal with a dance where the flowers are.

99900.q: How many eyes does a honeybee have?
99900.e: The bee has two big compound eyes. On top of that there are three small simple eyes on the top of its head.

99901.q: Why does a honeybee often die when it stings a person?
99901.e: The sting has tiny barbs. It gets stuck in human skin and tears off.
99901.m: The honeybee's sting gets stuck in our skin.

99902.q: What does a bumblebee's body look like?
99902.e: Bumblebees have a fat, round body with lots of hairs. The fur keeps them warm.
99902.m: Bumblebees are round and have thick fur.

99903.q: When can bumblebees still fly while honeybees stay in the hive?
99903.e: Bumblebees warm themselves up with their flight muscles. That is why they fly even in cool temperatures.
99903.m: Bumblebees fly even in cool weather.

99904.q: Who in a bumblebee colony survives the winter?
99904.e: In autumn the bumblebee colony dies. Only young queens survive the winter and start a new colony in spring.
99904.m: Only the young bumblebee queen survives the winter.

99905.q: Where do many bumblebees build their nest?
99905.e: Many bumblebees nest in old mouse holes or other hollows in the ground.
99905.m: Bumblebees often nest in holes in the ground.

99906.q: What noise do bumblebees make when they fly?
99906.e: The bumblebee's wings beat fast. This makes a deep buzzing sound.

99907.q: What do vegetable growers use bumblebees for in the greenhouse?
99907.e: Bumblebees shake the pollen out of tomato flowers with vibrations. This produces more tomatoes.
99907.m: Bumblebees pollinate the tomatoes in the greenhouse.

99908.q: Which group of animals do bumblebees belong to?
99908.e: Bumblebees are a group of bees. Like other bees, they collect nectar and pollen.

99909.q: How big is a bumblebee colony compared with a honeybee colony?
99909.e: A bumblebee colony usually has only a few hundred animals. A honeybee colony is many times bigger.
99909.m: Bumblebee colonies are much smaller than honeybee colonies.

99910.q: Roughly how many kinds of wild bee live in Switzerland?
99910.e: More than 600 kinds of wild bee are known in Switzerland. Many of them have become rare.
99910.m: About 600 kinds of wild bee live in Switzerland.

99911.q: How do most wild bees live?
99911.e: Most wild bees live alone. Each female builds her own nest.

99912.q: Where do many wild bees nest?
99912.e: Many kinds of wild bee dig their nests in the ground. They like open, sandy spots.
99912.m: Many wild bees nest in the ground.

99913.q: Which wild bee likes to nest in hollow plant stems?
99913.e: The red mason bee nests in hollow stems, cracks and small holes. That is why it likes moving into a bee hotel.
99913.m: The mason bee nests in cracks and tubes.

99914.q: Which food do we get from honeybees but not from wild bees?
99914.e: Wild bees also collect nectar and pollen. But they do not store honey that a beekeeper can harvest.
99914.m: Wild bees do not produce honey for the beekeeper.

99915.q: How can you help wild bees in the garden?
99915.e: Wild bees need lots of different flowers. A wild flower meadow gives them food.

99916.q: Which wild bee likes to dig its nest in sandy ground?
99916.e: Mining bees dig small tunnels in sandy ground. You often see little heaps of earth in front of the entrance.
99916.m: Mining bees dig their nests in the ground.

99917.q: Which wild bee collects plant hairs for its nest?
99917.e: The wool carder bee scrapes fine hairs off plants. It uses them to line its nest.
99917.m: The wool carder bee lines its nest with plant hairs.

99918.q: Which big wild bee is bluish black and gnaws tunnels into dead wood?
99918.e: The violet carpenter bee is one of the biggest bees in Europe. It nests in rotten wood.
99918.m: The carpenter bee gnaws its nest into dead wood.

99919.q: What do butterflies need in the morning before they can fly well?
99919.e: Butterflies warm themselves up in the sun. They often sit with their wings open to do this.
99919.m: Butterflies first soak up warmth from the sun.

99920.q: What hatches from a butterfly's egg?
99920.e: A caterpillar hatches from the egg. It eats a lot and grows fast.
99920.m: A caterpillar hatches from a butterfly egg.

99921.q: What does the caterpillar do before it becomes a butterfly?
99921.e: The caterpillar turns into a pupa. Inside the pupa it changes into a butterfly.
99921.m: Inside the pupa the caterpillar becomes a butterfly.

99922.q: Which butterfly is bright yellow and flies very early in spring?
99922.e: The brimstone spends the winter as an adult butterfly. On warm days in February or March it is already flying.
99922.m: The yellow brimstone flies very early in the year.

99923.q: Which butterfly has big eyespots on its wings?
99923.e: The peacock butterfly has four colourful spots that look like eyes. They startle birds.
99923.m: The peacock butterfly startles enemies with eyespots.

99924.q: What lies like fine dust on butterfly wings?
99924.e: Butterfly wings are covered in tiny scales. That is why you should not touch them.

99925.q: Which white butterfly likes to lay its eggs on cabbage plants?
99925.e: The caterpillars of the cabbage white eat cabbage leaves. That is why the butterfly lays its eggs on cabbage.
99925.m: The cabbage white lays its eggs on cabbage.

99926.q: What do butterflies use to taste whether a leaf is good?
99926.e: Butterflies have taste cells on their feet. This is how they test plants.

99927.q: Which butterfly has black and yellow wings with long tails at the back?
99927.e: The swallowtail has two long tails at the back, like the tail of a swallow.
99927.m: The swallowtail has tailed hind wings.

99928.q: Which animal do many hoverflies look like?
99928.e: Many hoverflies are striped yellow and black like wasps. This protects them from birds.

99929.e: Hoverflies have no sting. They only look dangerous.

99930.q: What are hoverflies especially good at in the air?
a: Flying across the sea without a break
99930.e: Hoverflies beat their wings very fast. This lets them stand almost still in the air.
99930.m: Hoverflies can stand still in the air.

99931.q: What do the larvae of many hoverflies eat?
99931.e: Many hoverfly larvae eat hundreds of aphids. That is why they are useful in the garden.

99932.q: How many wings does a hoverfly have?
99932.e: Hoverflies are flies. Flies have only one pair of wings, wasps have two pairs.

99933.q: Which group of animals do hoverflies belong to?
99933.e: Despite their stripes, hoverflies are true flies. You can tell by their short feelers.

99934.e: Adult hoverflies visit flowers. While doing so they pollinate the plants.
99934.m: Adult hoverflies live on nectar and pollen.

99935.q: Why are hoverflies striped like wasps?
99935.e: Birds avoid wasps because they sting. That is why they often leave the harmless hoverflies alone too.
99935.m: The wasp colours protect the hoverfly.

99936.q: What do the flowers of plants whose pollen is carried by the wind often look like?
99936.e: Plants that have the wind as a helper do not need to attract insects. That is why such flowers are inconspicuous.

99937.q: Which colour can bees not see?
99937.e: Bees see red only as a dark, almost black colour. That is why red flowers hardly catch their eye.

99938.q: Which light can bees see but we cannot?
99938.e: Bees see ultraviolet light. That is why flowers look different to them than to us.

99939.q: A yellow spot in a horse chestnut flower later turns red. What does that show?
a: There is no more nectar here.
There is especially a lot of nectar here.
99939.e: Young flowers have yellow spots and lots of nectar. Later the spot turns red, and bees prefer to fly to fresh flowers.
99939.m: In the horse chestnut, the colour of the spot shows whether there is nectar.

99940.q: Which flower colour do night-flying moths find best?
99940.e: In the twilight, white flowers stand out best. That is why moths find them easily.
99940.m: White flowers glow in the twilight.

99941.q: Which flower colours do bees especially like?
99941.e: Bees see blue and yellow very well. That is why they often fly to such flowers.
99941.m: Bees like flying to blue and yellow flowers.

99942.q: What colour is the centre of a daisy?
99942.e: The daisy has white petals on the outside and a yellow centre. The yellow centre attracts insects.
99942.m: The daisy has a yellow centre.

99943.q: Which creatures in America like flying to red flowers?
99943.e: Hummingbirds see red very well and drink nectar. Many red flowers in America are visited by them.
99943.m: Hummingbirds like flying to red flowers.

99944.q: How does a bumblebee notice that a flower has just been visited?
a: by the colour of the root
99944.e: Bumblebees leave a faint scent on the flower when they visit. Other bumblebees smell it and fly on.
99944.m: Bumblebees recognise visited flowers by their scent.

99945.q: What do bees use to smell the scent of flowers?
99945.e: The bee has lots of smell cells on its feelers. With them it can smell flowers very well.

99946.q: When do many flowers for moths smell strongest?
99946.e: Many flowers visited by moths only smell strongly in the evening. That is when these moths are out and about.
99946.m: Flowers for moths smell in the evening.

99947.q: Which creatures does a flower that stinks of rotten meat attract?
99947.e: Some flowers smell of rotten meat. This attracts flies, which pollinate them.

99948.q: Which climbing plant with long flower tubes attracts moths with its scent?
99948.e: Honeysuckle has long, narrow flower tubes. Moths get the nectar out with their long tongues.
99948.m: Honeysuckle attracts moths with its scent.

99949.q: What does a flower's scent tell insects?
99949.e: The scent says: there is nectar or pollen here. Insects learn such scents quickly.
99949.m: The scent of a flower reveals that there is food.

99950.q: In what weather can you usually smell flower scent especially well?
99950.e: Warmth makes the scent substances rise into the air more easily. That is why a garden smells strong on warm days.
99950.m: Flowers smell stronger in warm weather.

99951.q: How do bees remember good flowers?
a: by the weight of the leaves
by the length of the root
99951.e: Bees learn fast. They remember the scent and colour of flowers with lots of nectar.
99951.m: Bees remember the scent and colour of good flowers.

99952.q: Who lives in an insect hotel?
99952.e: In an insect hotel, wild bees and other insects find tubes and holes to lay their eggs in.
99952.m: Wild bees and other insects live in the insect hotel.

99953.q: Which way should an insect hotel face?
99953.e: Wild bees like it warm. A spot in the sun, ideally facing south, is perfect.
99953.m: An insect hotel belongs in a sunny spot.

99954.q: What is often put into an insect hotel?
99954.e: Hollow bamboo or reed tubes are ideal nesting tubes for wild bees.
99954.m: Hollow tubes are good homes for wild bees.

99955.q: What should the roof of an insect hotel protect against?
99955.e: The inside should stay dry. A small roof keeps the rain off.
99955.m: A roof keeps the insect hotel dry.

99956.q: What is needed near an insect hotel?
99956.e: Wild bees need food. Without flowers nearby, the hotel stays empty.
99956.m: An insect hotel needs flowers nearby.

99957.q: Into which material do you drill holes for an insect hotel?
99957.e: Good nesting holes are drilled into dry hardwood, for example beech or oak.
99957.m: Nesting holes are drilled into hardwood.

99958.q: Which bees especially like moving into an insect hotel?
99958.e: Mason bees nest in tubes and holes. That is why you often find them in an insect hotel.
99958.m: Mason bees like moving into the insect hotel.

99959.q: What should the inside of the holes in an insect hotel be like?
99959.e: Splinters can injure the delicate wings. That is why the holes should be smooth.
99959.m: Smooth holes protect the bees' wings.

99960.q: What do bees make honey from?
99960.e: Bees suck up nectar and bring it to the hive. There it is turned into honey.

99961.q: What is a person who keeps bees called?
99961.e: The beekeeper looks after their bee colonies and harvests the honey.

a: as a store for the winter
99962.e: In winter there are no flowers. The bees then eat their store of honey.
99962.m: Honey is the bees' winter store.

99963.q: Where do bees store the honey?
99963.e: The bees fill the honey into the cells of the honeycomb and seal them with wax.

99964.q: What often happens to runny honey after a while?
99964.e: Honey contains a lot of sugar. Over time the sugar forms crystals and the honey sets.

99965.q: What do bees make dark forest honey from?
99965.e: Aphids give off a sweet juice called honeydew. Bees collect it and make forest honey from it.
99965.m: Forest honey is made from honeydew.

99966.q: Which device does the beekeeper use to get the honey out of the combs?
99966.e: In the honey extractor the combs spin fast. This flings the honey out.
99966.m: The beekeeper spins the honey out of the combs.

99967.e: Honey consists mostly of sugar. That is why it tastes sweet.

99968.q: How many spots does the best-known ladybird in our country have?
99968.e: The seven-spot ladybird is very well known here. It has red wing cases with seven black spots.
99968.m: The best-known ladybird has seven spots.

99969.q: Do the spots show a ladybird's age?
99969.e: The number of spots depends on the species. It does not change with age.
99969.m: The spots show the species, not the age.

99970.q: What does a ladybird do when in danger?
a: It gives off a yellow juice
99970.e: The ladybird gives off a yellow, bitter juice from its legs. Enemies do not like the taste.
99970.m: In danger, the ladybird gives off a bitter juice.

99971.q: What does the ladybird larva eat?
99971.e: The larvae eat aphids too, and a great many of them. They look quite different from the beetles.

99972.q: How do ladybirds often spend the winter?
99972.e: In autumn, ladybirds look for sheltered places such as cracks or leaves. Often lots of them lie together.
99972.m: Ladybirds like spending the winter in groups.

99973.q: What do many people see the ladybird as?
a: as a sign of bad luck
99973.e: The ladybird is a popular lucky charm. In German it is even called the lucky beetle.
99973.m: The ladybird is seen as a lucky charm.

99974.e: The red colour warns birds: I don't taste good. That is why they rarely eat it.

99975.q: What shape are the cells of a honeycomb?
99975.e: The honeycomb cells have six corners. That way they fit next to each other without gaps.

99976.q: What is the opening that bees fly through into the hive called?
99976.e: The bees fly in and out through the entrance hole. Guard bees keep watch there.
99976.m: Bees fly into the hive through the entrance hole.

99977.q: What does the beekeeper use to calm the bees?
99977.e: Smoke makes the bees calmer. The beekeeper uses a smoker for this.
99977.m: The beekeeper calms the bees with smoke.

99978.q: What does the beekeeper wear for protection against stings?
99978.e: A beekeeper's veil protects the face and neck from bee stings.
99978.m: The beekeeper protects their face with a veil.

99979.q: How many queens normally live in a beehive?
99979.e: A bee colony normally has only one queen.
99979.m: A bee colony has one queen.

99980.q: How do bees keep warm in winter?
99980.e: In winter the bees huddle closely together. In this winter cluster they shiver their muscles and make warmth.
99980.m: In winter bees keep warm in a cluster.

99981.q: Roughly how many bees live in a strong bee colony in summer?
99981.e: In summer about 40,000 to 60,000 bees live in a strong colony.
99981.m: A strong bee colony has tens of thousands of bees in summer.

99982.q: What is the most energy-saving way to heat water for tea?
99982.e: In a kettle the heat is produced directly in the water. So less energy is lost than on the hob.
99982.m: A kettle saves electricity when heating water.

99983.q: Where does water boil at a lower temperature?
99983.e: On a high mountain the air pressure is lower. That is why water boils sooner there.
99983.m: On high mountains water boils sooner.

99984.q: What are the big bubbles in boiling water made of?
99984.e: At the bottom of the pan the water gets so hot that it turns into vapour. The vapour rises as a bubble.
99984.m: The bubbles in boiling water are water vapour.

99985.q: What is the white cloud above a cooking pot?
99985.e: The invisible vapour cools above the pot. It turns into tiny droplets, and you see them as a white cloud.
99985.m: The cloud above the pot is made of tiny droplets.

99986.q: Why do you put a lid on the pan when boiling water?
99986.e: The lid keeps the heat in the pan. So the water boils faster and you use less electricity.
99986.m: With a lid, water boils faster.

99987.q: Why does pasta go soft when you cook it?
99987.e: Dry pasta soaks up water in the hot water. It becomes soft and bigger.
99987.m: Pasta soaks up water when it cooks.

99988.q: Why are pan handles often made of plastic or wood?
99988.e: Plastic and wood are poor conductors of heat. So you can hold the pan without burning yourself.
99988.m: Handles made of wood or plastic stay cool.

99989.q: Why does food cook faster in a pressure cooker?
a: It gets hotter inside than usual.
99989.e: In the tightly closed pot the pressure rises. So the water only boils at a higher temperature, and the food cooks faster.
99989.m: In a pressure cooker it gets hotter than in an open pan.

99990.q: Which way do you turn the handle of a pan on the cooker?
99990.e: A handle sticking out over the edge of the cooker is easily knocked. Turned inwards, the pan is safer.
99990.m: Pan handles should be turned inwards.

99991.q: Why do you put baking powder in a cake mixture?
99991.e: Baking powder makes lots of tiny gas bubbles in the mixture. That makes the cake rise and turn out light.
99991.m: Baking powder makes a cake light.

99992.q: Which white powder is in baking powder?
99992.e: Baking powder contains bicarbonate of soda and a dry acid. Together with moisture, they make gas bubbles.
99992.m: Baking powder contains bicarbonate of soda.

99993.q: When does baking powder work most strongly in a mixture?
a: when it gets wet and hot
99993.e: Baking powder needs moisture and warmth. In the hot oven it makes the most bubbles.
99993.m: Baking powder works with moisture and heat.

99994.q: Does a cake mixture with baking powder have to rest for hours before baking?
a: No, it goes into the oven soon.
Yes, for at least three hours.
99994.e: Unlike yeast, baking powder doesn't need time to rise. You can bake the mixture straight away.
99994.m: A cake with baking powder is baked straight away.

99995.q: Why shouldn't you open the oven too early when baking a cake?
99995.e: Cold air flows into the oven. The gas bubbles in the still soft mixture shrink, and the cake sinks.
99995.m: If you open the oven too early, the cake may sink.

99996.q: Which bake do you usually use baking powder for?
99996.e: Loaf cakes and sponge cakes are usually baked with baking powder. Bread, on the other hand, is usually made with yeast.
99996.m: A loaf cake usually rises thanks to baking powder.

99997.q: What do you do with baking powder before it goes into the mixture?
99997.e: You mix the baking powder with the flour. That way it spreads evenly through the whole mixture.
99997.m: First mix baking powder with the flour.

99998.q: What does baking powder look like?
99998.e: Baking powder is a fine, white powder. You usually buy it in small sachets.
99998.m: Baking powder is a fine white powder.

99999.q: Which dough is a pizza base made from?
99999.e: Pizza dough is a yeast dough. The yeast makes it airy and soft.
99999.m: Pizza dough is a yeast dough.

100000.q: Where is the best place to let yeast dough rise?
100000.e: Yeast works best in the warmth. That is why you put the dough in a warm place.
100000.m: Yeast dough rises well in a warm place.

100001.q: What do you cover the bowl of yeast dough with while it rises?
a: With a pot full of water
100001.e: A cloth protects the dough from drying out and from draughts.
100001.m: Cover yeast dough with a cloth while it rises.

100002.q: Roughly how big should yeast dough be after rising?
100002.e: Many recipes say: let the dough rise until it has doubled in size.
100002.m: Well-risen yeast dough is about twice as big.

100003.q: What do you do to yeast dough to make it nice and stretchy?
a: knead it for a long time
100003.e: Kneading creates a stretchy network in the dough. That is why you knead yeast dough for several minutes.
100003.m: Kneading for a long time makes yeast dough stretchy.

100004.q: In what form do you often buy fresh yeast?
a: as a liquid in a bottle
100004.e: Fresh yeast comes as a soft, light brown cube in the chiller cabinet.
100004.m: You buy fresh yeast as a cube.

100005.q: What happens to yeast dough in the fridge?
100005.e: In the cold the yeast works only slowly. The dough then takes much longer to rise.
100005.m: In the fridge yeast dough rises only slowly.

100006.q: Which figure made of yeast dough do people eat in Switzerland around 6 December?
100006.e: On St Nicholas Day many families have a Grittibänz. It is a little man made of sweet yeast dough.
100006.m: Around St Nicholas Day people eat a Grittibänz.

100007.q: What happens to the egg white when you boil an egg?
100007.e: Raw egg white is runny and almost see-through. The heat makes it firm and white.
100007.m: When cooked, egg white goes firm and white.

100008.q: Roughly how long do you boil a hard-boiled egg?
100008.e: After about 10 minutes in boiling water, the white and the yolk are firm.
100008.m: A hard-boiled egg boils for about 10 minutes.

100009.q: Why do you put boiled eggs in cold water?
100009.e: Cooking carries on inside the hot egg. Cold water cools it down and stops the cooking.
100009.m: Cold water stops eggs cooking any further.

100010.q: How does a hard-boiled egg spin when you spin it on the table like a top?
100010.e: In a hard-boiled egg everything is solid and spins along with it. In a raw egg the inside sloshes about and slows it down.
100010.m: A hard-boiled egg spins like a top.

100011.q: Can a boiled egg become raw and runny again?
100011.e: Heat changes the egg white for ever. You can't undo the cooking.
100011.m: A boiled egg never becomes raw again.

100012.q: What is the yolk like in a soft-boiled egg?
100012.e: A soft-boiled egg is only cooked for a few minutes. The white is firm, but the yolk is still runny.
100012.m: In a soft-boiled egg the yolk is still runny.

100013.e: Butter is made from the fat in milk. That is why you use cream, which is rich in fat.

100014.q: What do you have to do with cream to make butter?
a: shake it for a long time
100014.e: Shaking or beating for a long time makes the little fat globules stick together. That makes butter.
100014.m: If you shake cream for a long time, you get butter.

100015.q: What is the liquid left over when making butter called?
100015.e: When making butter, the fat separates from the liquid. The liquid is called buttermilk.
100015.m: Buttermilk is left over when making butter.

100016.q: What device was used on farms in the past to make butter?
100016.e: In the butter churn the cream was pounded or turned for a long time until butter formed.
100016.m: In the past butter was made in a butter churn.

a: when the cows eat fresh grass
when it is kept in the dark
100017.e: Fresh grass contains a yellow colouring. It gets into the milk and makes the butter more yellow.
100017.m: Butter from cows out at pasture is especially yellow.

100018.q: Why is butter hard straight out of the fridge?
a: The fat goes solid in the cold.
100018.e: Butterfat goes solid in the cold. At room temperature it becomes soft and spreadable again.

100019.q: What forms first when you whip runny cream?
100019.e: First the cream goes stiff and you get whipped cream. If you keep whipping, you get butter.
100019.m: When whipped, cream first turns into whipped cream.

100020.q: What is butter mostly made of?
100020.e: Butter is more than 80 percent milk fat.

100021.q: Why does a corn kernel burst open in a hot pan?
a: The water inside turns to steam.
100021.e: There is a little water inside the kernel. It turns to steam, the pressure rises and the kernel bursts open.
100021.m: Steam inside a corn kernel makes it burst open.

100022.q: What noise does popcorn make when it bursts open?
100022.e: When the hard skin splits, there is a little pop. The word “pop” imitates this sound.
100022.m: Popcorn pops when it bursts open.

100023.q: How big is popcorn compared with the corn kernel?
100023.e: When it bursts, the inside of the kernel puffs up into a white foam. The popcorn is much bigger than the kernel.
100023.m: Popcorn is much bigger than the kernel.

100024.q: What colour is the burst-open inside of popcorn?
100024.e: The inside of the kernel turns into a white, airy foam that sets straight away.
100024.m: Popcorn is white and airy inside.

100025.q: Why do some corn kernels not burst open?
100025.e: Without enough water, too little steam forms. Kernels with a damaged skin often stay closed too.
100025.m: Kernels that are too dry don't pop.

100026.q: Why do you put a lid on the pan when making popcorn?
100026.e: The kernels jump up when they burst. The lid keeps them in the pan.
100026.m: The lid keeps the jumping popcorn in the pan.

100027.q: Where does popcorn originally come from?
100027.e: People in America were popping corn a very long time ago. From there, popcorn spread around the world.

100028.q: Which kind of corn do you need for popcorn?
100028.e: Popping corn has a particularly hard skin. That is why enough pressure builds up inside it for it to burst.
100028.m: For popcorn you need popping corn.

100029.q: Why do you need a hot pan for popcorn?
a: Only great heat makes enough steam.
The heat makes the kernels sweet.
100029.e: Only at great heat does the water in the kernel turn to steam quickly. In a lukewarm pan nothing happens.

100030.e: To make yoghurt you use milk. Tiny helpers turn it into yoghurt.

100031.e: When yoghurt is made, lactic acid forms from the milk sugar. It makes the yoghurt sour.

100032.q: What happens to the milk when making yoghurt?
100032.e: The acid makes the protein in the milk thicken. That is how runny milk becomes creamy yoghurt.
100032.m: When making yoghurt, the milk thickens.

100033.q: How warm should milk be for it to turn into yoghurt?
100033.e: The yoghurt bacteria work best at around 40 degrees. Then the milk turns into yoghurt within a few hours.

100034.q: What do you add to milk when you make your own yoghurt?
100034.e: The bacteria needed live in yoghurt. One spoonful is enough to start off a whole batch of milk.
100034.m: One spoonful of yoghurt is enough to start a batch.

100035.q: Which language does the word “yoghurt” come from?
100035.e: The word comes from the Turkish word “yoğurt”.

100036.q: What is the yellowish liquid that often collects on top of yoghurt called?
100036.e: The liquid on top is whey. You can simply stir it back in.
100036.m: The liquid on top of yoghurt is whey.

100037.q: Which appliance keeps the milk warm when making yoghurt?
100037.e: A yoghurt maker keeps the milk at the same warmth for hours. That way the bacteria can work well.
100037.m: A yoghurt maker keeps the milk warm.

100038.q: What does squash turn into if you put it in a mould in the freezer?
100038.e: The squash freezes in the mould. That makes an ice lolly on a stick.
100038.m: Frozen squash turns into an ice lolly.

100039.q: Why do strawberries go mushy after thawing?
a: Ice crystals have damaged them inside.
100039.e: When freezing, sharp ice crystals form in the fruit. They damage the cells, and the strawberry goes soft.
100039.m: Ice crystals make thawed fruit soft.

100040.q: What is it called when frozen food becomes soft again?
100040.e: Frozen food thaws in the warmth. It is best to let it thaw slowly in the fridge.
100040.m: Frozen food has to be thawed.

100041.q: What builds up over time on the walls of a freezer?
100041.e: Damp air gets in when you open it and freezes on the walls. That way a layer of ice grows.
100041.m: Over time a layer of ice grows in the freezer.

100042.q: Why do you keep stirring homemade ice cream while it freezes?
100042.e: Without stirring, big hard ice crystals form. Stirring keeps them small, and the ice cream becomes creamy.
100042.m: Stirring makes homemade ice cream creamy.

100043.q: Why can a damp tongue stick to very cold metal?
100043.e: Cold metal draws heat from the tongue quickly. The saliva freezes and sticks the tongue on.
100043.m: Your tongue can freeze onto ice-cold metal.

100044.q: Why are frozen peas as hard as little stones?
a: The water inside them is frozen.
100044.e: Peas contain a lot of water. In the freezer this water turns to ice, which is why they are hard.
100044.m: Frozen water makes peas rock hard.

100045.q: What helps sugar dissolve faster in tea?
100045.e: When you stir, fresh water keeps reaching the sugar. So it dissolves faster.

100046.q: Which sugar dissolves fastest in water?
100046.e: Icing sugar is ground very finely. The many tiny grains dissolve very quickly.

100047.q: How can you tell that dissolved sugar is still in the water?
100047.e: You can't see the sugar any more, but it is still there. You can tell from the sweet taste.
100047.m: Dissolved sugar makes the water sweet.

100048.q: What happens if you keep adding more and more sugar to a glass of water?
a: At some point sugar stays at the bottom.
There is more and more water.
100048.e: Water can only take in a certain amount of sugar. After that, the rest stays at the bottom as grains.
100048.m: Water can't dissolve an endless amount of sugar.

100049.q: What forms when you heat sugar strongly in a pan?
100049.e: The sugar melts and turns golden brown. That makes caramel.

100050.q: Does sugar dissolve in cooking oil?
a: Yes, but only after an hour.
100050.e: Sugar dissolves well in water, but not in oil. In oil the grains stay visible, even if you stir.

100051.q: What do you call a liquid in which sugar has completely dissolved?
100051.e: When a substance spreads completely through water, it is called a solution. Sugar water is a solution.

100052.q: What is another name for table salt?
100052.e: Table salt is also called cooking salt, because you use it when cooking.
100052.m: Table salt is also called cooking salt.

100053.q: Why do you put salt in the water for spaghetti?
100053.e: The salt makes the spaghetti tastier. It doesn't make the water boil faster.
100053.m: Salt in the cooking water seasons the pasta.

100054.q: What happens if you sprinkle salt on cucumber slices?
100054.e: The salt draws water out of the cucumber slices. After a short time they are lying in a little puddle.
100054.m: Salt draws water out of cucumbers.

100055.q: What was salt especially needed for in the past, when there were no fridges?
100055.e: Salt draws water out of meat. That makes it harder for germs to multiply, and the meat keeps longer.

100056.q: Which substance is often added to table salt in Switzerland?
100056.e: Salt with iodine has been available in Switzerland since 1922. The body needs iodine for the thyroid gland.
100056.m: Swiss table salt often contains iodine.

100057.q: What is salt dough for crafts made from?
100057.e: For salt dough you mix flour, salt and water. The figures are dried in the oven and go hard.
100057.m: Salt dough is made of flour, salt and water.

100058.q: In which place in the canton of Vaud can you visit a salt mine?
100058.e: Salt has been mined in Bex for centuries. Visitors can ride a little train into the tunnels.
100058.m: You can visit a salt mine in Bex.

100059.e: The sour substance in vinegar is called acetic acid.

100060.q: What is vinegar often used for in the home?
100060.e: Vinegar dissolves limescale. You can use it, for example, to remove limescale marks in the bathroom.

100061.q: What happens to the shell of a raw egg that lies in vinegar for two days?
100061.e: Eggshells are made of lime. The acid in the vinegar dissolves the lime, leaving an egg with a soft skin.

100062.q: What do you mix with vinegar for a simple salad dressing?
100062.e: A simple salad dressing is made of vinegar, oil, salt and a little mustard.
100062.m: For a simple salad dressing you mix vinegar and oil.

100063.q: What turns wine into vinegar over time?
100063.e: Vinegar bacteria turn the alcohol in wine into acid. That is how wine becomes vinegar.

100064.q: What happens when sherbet powder goes into water?
100064.e: In water the substances in the sherbet powder react with each other. Lots of bubbles form.

100065.q: Which gas forms in water from sherbet powder?
100065.e: In water the powder produces carbon dioxide. The gas rises in bubbles.
100065.m: The bubbles in fizzy sherbet water are carbon dioxide.

100066.q: Why does sherbet powder tingle on your tongue?
100066.e: Saliva makes the powder damp. Then lots of tiny bubbles form on your tongue.
100066.m: Sherbet powder fizzes in your mouth and tingles.

100067.q: Why must sherbet powder be kept dry?
a: Moisture makes it fizz too early.
100067.e: Even a little moisture starts the reaction. Then the powder won't fizz properly later.
100067.m: Sherbet powder belongs in a dry place.

100068.q: What are tablets called that fizz and dissolve in water?
100068.e: Effervescent tablets work like sherbet powder. In water they fizz and dissolve.

100069.q: Why does sherbet powder taste sweet?
a: It contains only bicarbonate of soda.
100069.e: As well as the fizzing substances, sherbet powder also contains sugar. That is why it tastes sweet.

100070.q: Which drink contains the same gas as fizzing sherbet water?
100070.e: The same gas is dissolved in sparkling mineral water. That is why it fizzes when you open it.
